status_rule: knocked_down if answered or tension not real or not feasible in a week; survives if open/partly answered and an expert cannot predict; else weakened

verified.question: Why do online early-exit rules stop so far short of the hindsight stop point: when an answer has formed, is whether it will later change already decided by the prefix (so a better signal can find it) or decided by later sampling (so no signal can)?

closest_papers.title: The Detection-Extraction Gap: Models Know the Answer Before They Can Say It
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Closest direct measurement of within-prefix answer dispersion under FREE continuations. Appendix L stores all 8 continuations per prefix and reports pairwise self-agreement: MATH-500, Qwen3-32B-Think, solvable problems (n=83) 98.8% / 99.1% / 98.8% at 10% / 30% / 50% prefix, wrong problems (n=17) 67.1% / 78.7% / 86.9%; GPQA, Qwen3-8B-Think, solvable (n=40) 60.5% / 64.1% / 71.2%, wrong (n=10) 44.8% / 52.0% / 52.6%. Quote: "On MATH-500, solvable problems have near-perfect self-agreement (99%)". So on solvable MATH problems the final answer of a free continuation is already nearly fixed at a 10% prefix (flip probability per prefix must be near 0 or 1), while on GPQA with an 8B model it is widely dispersed. That gives the likely shape of the card's answer: it follows the problem's self-consistency, not a single prefix-vs-sampling split. BAEE in the same paper is already the card's outcome-B design (forks from a prefix plus agreement as the exit rule, total tokens up 3-5x). Leaves open: N=8, 50-100 problems, fixed 10%-grid prefixes not the first forced-readout fixed point, no per-prefix flip distribution, no variance split, no temperature ablation, no single-pass probe ("a direct comparison on the same model is future work"). Card correction: Eq. 2 defines psc as the fraction of continuations that are CORRECT, not fork agreement, though App. E.1 says "psc measures self-agreement rather than accuracy".

closest_papers.title: It's the Problem, Not the Path: Budget and Difficulty Confounds in LLM Reasoning Trajectories
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Does the decomposition the card lacks, for correctness rather than flips. Splits pooled probe AUROC into between-problem and within-problem parts: pooled 0.849 [0.735, 0.919], within problem 0.496 [0.466, 0.527] ("within problem it is statistically indistinguishable from chance at all ten anchors"); a trace-blind difficulty proxy reaches 0.873 on 192K DeepSeek-R1 generations. Conclusions: "High pooled probe AUROCs cannot by themselves establish within-attempt information"; "Within-attempt information therefore exists but is small on average"; "Accumulated reasoning is predominantly compute compression." It samples m=4 continuations from log-spaced prefix anchors and compares them with from-scratch restarts. This directly undermines the card: its 'between-prefix share' would mostly be between-PROBLEM variance, and a fork-supervised probe (outcome A) would mostly learn problem difficulty. Leaves open: two small 4-bit models (Gemma-4 E4B, Ministral-3 3B), 89 MATH problems, outcome is correctness not answer change, anchors are token positions not answer formation, no link to exit rules or the oracle.

closest_papers.title: The Potential of CoT for Reasoning: A Closer Look at Trace Dynamics
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Measures the card's per-prefix quantity with far more forks than the card plans: potential = "the probability of success of the model when sampling conditioned on a given partial chain of the CoT", N=128 continuations per prefix, temperature 0.6, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1, Qwen3-0.6B/32B. Curves are non-monotone ("Typical chain-of-thought exhibits quite erratic potentials"; monotonicity 15-45% on AIME-2024; tangents, drops of at least 30%, in 5-41% of traces). Appendix A.4 defines 'stability' with the chain's own final answer as target ("Stability measures how determined the final answer is throughout the reasoning process") and finds "models can become convinced very early on in their reasoning about wrong answers". Leaves open: stability is shown for two example curves only, with no distribution of values, no conditioning on answer formation, no variance split, and no early-exit analysis.

closest_papers.title: Early Stopping in Large Reasoning Models: A Survey and Empirical Audit of Efficiency and Reliability
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Audits exit methods against a hindsight oracle on one replayed trace per problem and tests a sampling-noise null: at random exit positions it draws eight independent forced answers and fits a monotone null; "Randomized exit experiments confirm that these reversals exceed those expected from stochastic decoding noise alone" (average excess reversal 1.2087%, up to 3.55% for gpt-oss-20b on TruthfulQA). Oracle 0.894 vs DEER 0.773 on gpt-oss-20b math/science. On the gap it only says "Current methods still struggle to identify reliable stopping positions while keeping verification costs low" and that results "do not establish a universal gap to an all-position oracle". Leaves open: the eight samples are forced answers, not free continuations; no per-prefix flip probability; no between/within split. Read to 100k of 120k characters.

closest_papers.title: Constructing Pareto Frontiers of Optimal Reasoning Termination Methods for Overthinking in Reasoning Models
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Computes the oracle the card quotes, from 16 forced answers per position on one fixed trace: "only the answer is resampled, while the reasoning prefix remains fixed"; "The 16 completions at each position are answer generations conditioned on the retained prefix; they are not independently generated reasoning trajectories." States that offline frontiers "do not specify an online policy that can access the same information before the trajectory is complete" and that its probe-sensitivity check "does not establish that 16 probes recover an infinite-probe optimum". Does not explain why online rules miss the oracle and never forks the reasoning.

closest_papers.title: Settle: Learning When to Stop Reasoning
closest_papers.what_it_shows: A prefix-only stop score already predicts answer persistence better than the card's 0.6-0.7 probe figures in the pooled case: AUROC 0.831 / 0.838 overall (base model's native score 0.532, elapsed tokens 0.618), but among currently correct prefixes at identical token counts only 0.695 / 0.706 for 'stays correct at every later readout' (base 0.495). 40% fewer tokens for 0.5 points on MATH-500, Qwen3-4B. Labels are greedy forced readouts on one completed trace sampled at temperature 1.0; no forks, no oracle comparison, no analysis of sampling noise. The 0.70 conditional figure is consistent with either a weak signal or a noise ceiling, so it does not settle the card's question.

closest_papers.title: Stable Answers, Unfinished Reasoning: Why Self-Consensus Is Not a Safe Early-Exit Signal
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Card's source for abandoned consensus. Uses one frozen trajectory per problem and offline forced probes; explains premature stops by elicitation, not sampling: "a probe elicits an answer rather than reading one". Limitations: they "do not run a controlled experiment that manipulates independence directly"; error counts are not "compared against a chance baseline". No forks of the reasoning, no predictor of abandonment. Read to 100k of 127k characters.

closest_papers.title: Concise-9B (arXiv 2611.02278)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Card's source for the hindsight stop point. The fixed point is defined on one trace with greedy forced readouts and the trace's own final answer. Attributes the miss to missing signal without testing sampling: "early agreement is common on answers that the model later revises, so agreement alone does not tell a fixed answer from a provisional one"; says the hindsight bound "is not a deployable rule". Sampling for Qwen3.5: temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, presence penalty 1.5. Never resamples from the fixed point.

closest_papers.title: Beyond the Commitment Boundary: Probing Epiphenomenal Chain-of-Thought in Large Reasoning Models
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Single-pass probe for the commitment boundary: detection 92% / early-fire 6% (gpt-oss-20b), 98% / 2% (Qwen3-14B), 62% / 16% (gemma-4-26B) on MATH-500; probe exit keeps 89% of full-CoT accuracy at 39% token saving (k=1), 98% at 26% (k=5). Boundary is defined by greedy forced-answer confidence on one trace; the paper says this "ignores the full predictive distribution" and that "Sampling-based or distribution-level extensions of the framework are a natural direction for future work". So the sampling question is named as open, not answered.

closest_papers.title: Are language models aware of the road not taken? Token-level uncertainty and hidden state dynamics
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Existence proof of the card's outcome-A design at toy scale: a linear probe on the hidden state is trained to predict the outcome distribution of resampled continuations (Forking Paths style), reaching about 0.11 KL versus 0.85 for a majority-class baseline and 1.53 uniform. Llama-3.2-3B with zero-shot CoT (not a reasoning model), probing on 10 AQuA examples. No early exit, no flip target.

closest_papers.title: Large Language Models Decide Early and Explain Later
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Qwen3-4B at temperature 0.6, single trace with forced answer completion at each step; a logistic probe gate saves about 500 tokens at under 2% accuracy drop against roughly 550-760 tokens generated after the last answer switch. Reports no AUC for predicting later switches, no forks, and does not say whether switches are predictable or random.

closest_papers.title: Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
closest_papers.what_it_shows: 100 rollouts per sentence on R1-Distill-Qwen-14B (temperature 0.6), 20 MATH problems chosen to be "correctly solved 25-75% of the time". Shows outcome probability moves sharply at particular sentences, but the analysis explicitly drops the regime the card cares about: it uses "only sentences before the model has converged on an answer" (same response in over 98% of resamples). No flip-after-formation statistics.

closest_papers.title: Forking Fast: Efficiently Estimating Uncertainty Dynamics in Text Generation
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Resamples continuations at every token (Llama-3-8B) or sentence (R1-Distill-Llama-8B) on 100 tinyMMLU questions; outcome distributions are flat or slowly drifting for long stretches "except at key forking points which have sharp changes", and apparent step-to-step noise is "largely an artifact of sampling" (reconstruction error falls about as 1/sqrt(S)). Supports a prefix-decided, piecewise-constant picture in general, but gives no share of prefixes near 0/1, nothing at answer formation, nothing on exit.

closest_papers.title: SABER: Stability-Aware Early Exit for LLM Reasoning via Adversarial Branch Probing
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Card's own prior-search hit. Branches are two forced-answer prompts (neutral and 'my reasoning was incorrect') with continuations capped at 10 tokens, "rather than full trajectory rollouts". No per-prefix flip rate, no AUC, no oracle-gap explanation. Not an answer.

closest_papers.title: When Does Learning to Stop Help? A Cost-Aware Study of Early Exits in Reasoning Models
closest_papers.what_it_shows: One greedy forced probe per checkpoint; classifies trajectories (early-solved, beneficial thinking, harmful overthinking, unsolved, oscillating) and shows a scalar signal "is systematically fooled by oscillation". No oracle comparison, no free forks, no noise-versus-signal analysis.

closest_papers.title: Entropy After </Think> for reasoning model early exiting
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Pass@1 per prefix from 128 forced answers after a manually appended </think>, not free continuations. Describes three phases (Pass@1 near 0, then correct "by chance", then always correct). 12-22% token saving. No oracle gap analysis.

closest_papers.title: Token Budget Saturation (arXiv 2607.21433)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Abstract only. Card correction: the AUC 0.608 (+/-0.080, permutation p=0.063) is for predicting whether an R1-Distill-Qwen-7B generation finishes within the token budget on AIME, not for exit or answer flips. It is weak support for a 'probe plateau'.

answered.remaining_gap:
No paper found forks free continuations at the first forced-readout fixed point (and later checkpoints) of a reasoning trace, reports the distribution of per-prefix flip probability, or splits flip variance into parts. No paper ties such a split to the gap between online exit rules and the hindsight stop point. In that narrow sense the card's measurement is not in print.

What is in print makes the answer much more predictable than the card claims, and weakens three parts of it:

1. The two-way split (prefix versus later sampling) is confounded by problem identity. 2609.03436 shows probes that look predictive pooled (AUROC 0.849) are at chance within a problem (0.496), and a trace-blind difficulty proxy reaches 0.873. A high between-prefix share in the card's experiment would mostly be between-problem variance, which is self-consistency of the problem, already known. The card's stop rule (share above 0.8) would fire for the wrong reason.

2. The likely shape of the answer follows from 2604.06613 Appendix L: eight free continuations from a 10% prefix agree pairwise 98.8% on solvable MATH-500 problems (Qwen3-32B-Think) but 60.5% on GPQA (Qwen3-8B-Think). So flips are close to prefix- or problem-decided on easy math and heavily sampling-dispersed on hard science with a small model. An expert who has read this would predict 'it depends on the problem's self-consistency', not be unable to predict.

3. Both designs the card points to already exist: fork-and-agree exit is BAEE (2604.06613, at 3-5x total tokens), and a probe trained on fork outcome distributions is shown at toy scale in 2511.04527; single-pass boundary probes with 92-98% detection are in 2606.13603, and Settle (2609.38997) reaches AUROC 0.83 pooled, 0.70 conditional on currently-correct.

The residue that stays untouched and unpredictable: within a problem, at the point where a forced readout first stabilises, does the specific sampled path carry any information about a later answer change beyond the problem-level answer distribution (a three-way split: between problem, between path within problem, within prefix), for 8-30B reasoning models at their recommended hot sampling settings. A related untested point is whether the hindsight stop point (0.35-0.44x in 2611.02278; 14.2% oracle budget in 2610.13570) is inflated by selecting on one sampled path, since both are computed on a single trace with forced readouts; 2611.00166 only tests a noise null on forced answers (average excess reversal 1.2087%). 2606.13603 names sampling-based extensions as future work.

Card corrections: 2607.21433's AUC 0.608 predicts budget convergence, not flips; 2604.06613's psc is a correctness fraction in its Eq. 2; 2602.14903 (N=128 continuations per prefix, with a 'stability' variant targeting the chain's own answer) and 2609.03436 are missing from the card's prior search and are closer than anything it lists.

evidence_checks.claim: Concise-9B (2611.02278): the hindsight stop point is at 0.35-0.44x tokens, three agreeing forced answers cost 2.4-9.2 points, and 59% of wrong traces also have an early fixed point.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: The quote is in the abstract: "Stopping each trace there would keep every answer at 0.35–0.44×" and "stopping as soon as three consecutive forced answers agree costs the base model 2.4–9.2 points". Setting: Qwen3.5-9B, one trace per problem, forced greedy readouts every 2,048 thinking tokens, temperature 1.0, presence penalty 1.5. The fixed point is defined against that trace's own final answer, so it is not a stopping time. The 59% is misread: Table 4 gives the share of thinking tokens after the fixed point in wrong traces (59% on both sets), not the share of wrong traces; the trace share fixed before the end is 88% and 83%. On the hard set the three-agree rule already reaches 0.45x tokens against 0.44x for the fixed point, so the gap there is 9.2 accuracy points, not tokens. The paper gives no count of how often an agreed answer is later revised and does no forking.

evidence_checks.claim: Pareto Frontiers (2610.13570): oracle budget to match full thinking is 14.2% for dynamic early exit, 35.0% fixed budgets, 71.4% dynamic routing.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: The numbers are there, but they are budget caps at which an offline oracle frontier first matches the reference accuracy (72.33% macro), over six other models (GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3-4B/30B-A3B, R1-Distill 7/14/32B), not realised costs. The oracle picks the best measured position per trajectory from 16 sampled answer probes, so it selects on probe noise. The paper itself shows the measured overthinking ratio rises as probes are reduced (74.69% at 4 probes, 69.09% at 8, 66.22% at 12, 64.34% at 16) and says it "does not establish that 16 probes recover an infinite-probe optimum". So part of the 14.2% is selection on noise by construction. It is not the same quantity as the 2611.02278 fixed point, and the paper gives no numeric gap between real methods and the frontier (figure only).

evidence_checks.claim: Stable Answers, Unfinished Reasoning (2609.09989): 736 of 1,500 trajectories agreed on an answer they later abandoned; 84.2% still ended correct; 155 of 216 non-terminal stops commit a wrong answer to a trajectory that would have reached the right one.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: All three numbers are in sections 4.1 and 4.4 (R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on MATH500, forced boxed-answer probes every 64 tokens on a single frozen trajectory; the 216 are from 3,420 trajectories at W=12). But the source reads against the card's 'sampling wandering' interpretation. Its explanation is that an early probe forces an answer out of unfinished reasoning: "what repeats across probes can be a placeholder that looks stable while the trajectory keeps correcting itself". Of the 216 stops, 155 are wrong-to-right, 45 wrong-to-wrong and only 16 right-to-wrong. That is directed progress, not a random walk between answers. No forks, no per-prefix flip probability. DEER as a control loses 0.33 pp at 28.2% saving.

evidence_checks.claim: DEER (2504.15895): accuracy +0.9 to +4.8 points with 19.1% to 42.9% shorter sequences.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Quote confirmed: "achieving accuracy improvements of 0.9 to 4.8 points while reducing sequence length by 19.1% to 42.9% compared to vanilla models" (R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen3-14B, QwQ-32B; five benchmarks). Different models and benchmarks from the Concise-9B fixed point, so '19-43% versus 0.35-0.44x' is not a same-setting gap. Other online rules report more: GLOBE (2610.25970 abstract) 49.7% fewer output tokens with accuracy "comparable to Full CoT"; Reasoning Theater (2603.05488) keeps 97% of accuracy at 68% saving on MMLU and 50% on GPQA-Diamond.

evidence_checks.claim: Detection-Extraction Gap (2604.06613): at a 10% prefix Qwen3-32B-Think is 70% recoverable by free continuation and 34% correct under forced extraction; BAEE truncates 70-78% of serial generation and total tokens rise 3-5x.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Confirmed (N=8 continuations, threshold 0.75, MATH-500). The card omits that this paper already contains fork-agreement data that answers most of the question. Appendix L at f=0.10: on MATH-500 with 32B-Think, solvable problems average 98.8% self-agreement among the 8 forks and wrong problems 67.1% (only 2 of 17 reach 6/8); on GPQA-Diamond with 8B-Think, solvable problems average 60.5% and wrong problems 44.8%. So fork outcomes are near-deterministic where the model reliably solves the problem and split where it does not. The paper's cold-start comparison numbers conflict between appendices (SC-8 on MATH-500 32B-Think: 87.6% in Appendix M, 71.8% in Appendix P).

evidence_checks.claim: Single-pass exit probes plateau at modest discrimination: AUC above 0.7 (2504.05419) and 0.608 (2607.21433), read as a possible sampling-noise ceiling.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Both quotes exist, but they are not the same target and neither predicts whether an answer will change. 2504.05419 probes correctness of an intermediate answer; its tables show 0.82 (GSM8K), 0.84 (MATH), 0.67 (KnowLogic) and "over 0.9" for R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on AIME, so it is not a 0.6-0.7 plateau. 2607.21433 predicts whether a run converges within budget from token 150 of the trace, AUC 0.608 (±0.080) with permutation p=0.063: a very early, underpowered probe on a different question. Probes aimed at the right target do better: TERMINATOR (2603.12529) trains a final-layer probe on hindsight first-answer positions and reports it is "notably close" to the hindsight-optimal length with median position error 7; Reasoning Theater (2603.05488) decodes the final answer from prefixes at 87.98% macro accuracy on MMLU. There is no cross-paper plateau to explain.

evidence_checks.claim: Prior-answer search: nobody splits the chance of a later answer change into a prefix part and a sampling part; fork-supervised probes and fork-and-vote are open designs.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: I found no paper reporting the exact variance share, and 2606.30852 and 2603.05488 both state they do not resample continuations. But the pieces exist. Thought Anchors (2506.19143) runs 100 rollouts per sentence prefix on problems solved 25-75% of the time and shows prefix accuracy drifting, jumping at particular sentences, and then converging ("gives the same response in >98% of resamples"). 2604.06613 Appendix L gives fork agreement by problem type. Both designs are already built: BLADE (2607.28966, abstract) trains exit probes on labels from repeated answer completions per prefix and saves 24.8% (Qwen3-8B) and 15.8% (Qwen3-4B); BAEE in 2604.06613 is fork-and-vote and costs 3-5x total tokens; SABER (2608.27963) samples k=4 short branches per prefix at 3.8% probe overhead for 30.2-39.8% saving. 2606.30852 reports that on AIME "67.8% of trajectories never become correct at any budget" and no prefix signal certifies aggressive stopping, while on early-solved sets a plain confidence exit wins. My arXiv API and Semantic Scholar searches were rate-limited (429), so the search rested on three WebSearch calls plus direct reads; 'no exact decomposition found' is likely, not established.

premise.predicted_answer: Neither A nor B: a mixture split by problem difficulty, and I would bet 4:1 on it. On problems the model reliably solves, the per-prefix flip probability sits near 0 (readout already right) or near 1 (readout was a premature placeholder and nearly every fork finishes the derivation). On problems where independent traces disagree, it is intermediate and the forks split roughly as cold-start samples do. Published fork data already show this: 98.8% fork agreement on solvable MATH-500 problems against 67.1% on wrong ones and 44.8-60.5% on GPQA-Diamond (2604.06613 Appendix L), and Thought Anchors' 100-rollout curves on 25-75% problems. The proposed between-prefix share will therefore land in an uninformative middle that tracks the benchmark's difficulty mix. A toy mix of 80% of prefixes at p=0.02 and 20% at p=0.5 gives a share of 0.36; spreading the hard 20% uniformly over [0,1] gives 0.52. The number moves with dataset choice, not with anything about the model, and it selects neither design. I also expect trial-answer confidence to predict flips at AUC around 0.8, below the card's 0.9 stop line, because confidence mostly tracks difficulty.
premise.strongest_argument_it_is_boring:
1. The gap is partly true by definition. The hindsight point in 2611.02278 is the first readout after which that one sampled trace never changes, defined with knowledge of its final answer. That is not a stopping time, so any randomness at all leaves a gap. The 2610.13570 oracle picks the best of noisy 16-probe estimates per trajectory, and the paper shows its numbers inflate as probes get noisier. 'Some of the gap is unreachable' needs no experiment.

2. The gap is not one gap. 0.35-0.44x is Qwen3.5-9B with a 2,048-token cadence; 14.2% is an accuracy-matching budget cap over six other models; 19-43% is DEER on three more. Inside 2611.02278 the crude three-agree rule already reaches 0.45x tokens on the hard set; what it loses is 9.2 points. Better rules claim about 50% (GLOBE, Reasoning Theater on GPQA-Diamond) and TERMINATOR reports landing within a median of 7 positions of its hindsight label.

3. The card's reason for uncertainty misreads its own sources. 2609.09989 explains abandoned agreed answers as placeholders forced out of unfinished reasoning (155 wrong-to-right against 16 right-to-wrong), which is prefix-decided progress, not wandering. The '0.6-0.7 probe plateau' mixes a correctness probe that reaches 0.82-0.9+ with an underpowered convergence probe at token 150.

4. The qualitative answer is in print. Fork agreement is near 100% on problems the model solves and split on problems it does not (2604.06613 Appendix L; Thought Anchors). Self-consistency only works because hard problems have split answer distributions under temperature 0.6-1.0, so sampling-decided on hard problems is a known fact.

5. Both designs exist and their results are known. A probe trained on repeated completions per prefix (BLADE) saves 15.8-24.8%. Fork-and-vote (BAEE) truncates 70-78% of serial tokens but costs 3-5x in total, so outcome B's 'replace the tail with a few short forks' is not an efficiency gain: forks must run to an answer. Outcome B's fallback, 'train it away as Concise-9B does', is already done.

6. The measured statistic cannot choose between designs because it is dominated by between-problem difficulty, which is available without any prefix signal.
premise.sharpened_question: Weak residue only; I would not commit to it without first resolving the conflicting cold-start numbers in 2604.06613 (Appendix M against Appendix P). On problems where the model's independent traces disagree (per-question accuracy 25-75%), does the prefix at answer formation carry information about the final answer beyond the question itself? Concretely: is the fork answer distribution from the first stable readout sharper than the cold-start distribution for the same question, and does a probe on the prefix state predict fork outcomes better than a probe on the question alone? If not, every exit signal is a difficulty estimate available at the prompt, and early exit on hard problems reduces to budget routing by difficulty. If so, there is prefix-specific signal worth a probe on exactly the problems where today's rules lose accuracy. Caveats: 2604.06613 partly addresses this (prefix adds about +1.4 pp over cold-start SC-8 on MATH-500, but is called essential on GPQA-Diamond), and 2606.30852 already reports that no prefix signal certifies aggressive stopping on AIME, so a strong researcher would lean towards 'little beyond difficulty' on math and be unsure on GPQA-style sets.

feasible.first_week_experiment:
Redesigned, because the card's version (MATH-like problems, anchor at the first three-agree point, no baseline) would return "prefix-decided" for trivial reasons.

**Day 0, no GPU**
1. Use the question-level decomposition from the rollouts on disk (done above) as the baseline.
2. Stream uzaymacar/math-rollouts and compute, per sentence prefix, the fork distribution of the final answer and the forced-answer readout for R1-Distill-8B and 14B. This gives the full decomposition on two models before any job runs.

**Days 1-2, screening (Qwen3-8B primary)**
- Settings: T=0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, no presence penalty, so forks are exact samples of the base process.
- Pool: about 400 candidates (MATH-500 levels 4-5, AIME24, AIME25; GPQA as a non-math check).
- 16 cold-start samples each; 16K cap, 32K for AIME.
- Keep about 100 problems whose cold-start majority share is 0.2-0.8, plus 50 deterministic controls.
- Four of the 16 samples become base traces; the rest are the question-only baseline.

**Days 2-4, anchors and forks**
- Greedy forced readouts every 512 tokens: close thinking, append "The final answer is \boxed{", at most 32 tokens.
- Locate per trace: t1 (first three agreeing readouts), t* (the hindsight fixed point as defined in 2611.02278), 0.5·t*, and t* plus a quarter of the remainder.
- At each anchor: 16 free continuations to the end (one warm request, then n=16 on the cached prefix) and 16 sampled forced readouts for readout noise.
- Volume: about 600 traces x 4 anchors x 16 forks (38k forks) on Qwen3-8B; half that on Qwen3.5-9B once the presence-penalty fix is in.

**Day 4, hidden states**
- HF forward over the anchors, last-token residual at 4 layers.

**Metrics**
- M1: variance share V = 1 - E[p̂(1-p̂)·n/(n-1)] / (p̄(1-p̄)), for "final answer differs from the readout" and for "final answer correct", at each anchor. Report it against V at the question alone; the quantity of interest is the increment over the question and the residual at t*.
- M2: share of t* anchors where at least 15 of 16 forks keep the readout answer, split into mixed and deterministic problems.
- M3: tokens versus accuracy for the rule "stop at the first anchor where fork-estimated flip probability is below tau", against the hindsight point and the three-agree rule. This is the reachable bound.
- M4: probe AUROC against fork flip rate: pooled, within-problem, and against a difficulty-only baseline. Compare with the maximum AUROC the p_i distribution allows.

**Controls**
- Cold-start baseline.
- Truncation kept as a third outcome.
- Exchangeability test: the base trace's own final answer should look like one more fork.
- Shuffled-prefix-within-problem control.
- Problem-grouped cross-validation for the probes.
feasible.result_that_kills_it:
Any one of these, all visible by day 3:

1. **The question decides.** The question-only share is about 0.8 or more on the screened pool and fewer than about 40 of 400 problems have mixed cold-start outcomes among finished samples. Then there is no within-question answer variance to decompose at this model size. This is already what the on-disk 4B rollouts show (0.93 among finished samples; 2-3 mixed problems) and what two papers imply:
   - 2604.06613, as summarised from its Appendix M: cold-start SC-8 nearly matches psc@10% on MATH-500 (+1.4 pp); Appendix H: replacing 30% of prefix tokens moves psc from 97.5% to 94.8%.
   - 2609.03436: "exactly one prefix-limited cell in the entire dataset" (1 of 178); a trace-blind difficulty proxy reaches AUROC 0.873; a published early-window probe is 0.849 pooled but 0.496 within problem.
2. **The gap is readout spacing.** On mixed problems, at least 15 of 16 forks at t* keep the readout answer in over 90% of anchors, and finer-spaced readouts already reach t* within one interval. Then the gap to hindsight is the placeholder and spacing problem 2609.09989 already describes (first consensus "correct 27.5% of the time versus 85.2% at completion").
3. **The card's own stop.** Between-prefix share above 0.8 and trial-answer confidence predicts flips with AUROC above 0.9.
4. **Forks are not valid samples.** The exchangeability test fails on Qwen3-8B. The method is then invalid until fixed, not the question dead.

Honest prior: outcome 1 or 2 is more likely than not on MATH-type data at 8-9B. The card's "low confidence" expert prediction should be "moderately confident: prefix- or question-decided, and flips are mostly placeholder readouts".
feasible.result_that_makes_it_a_paper:
**Main paper outcome: the hindsight point is partly luck**
- On problems with mixed cold-start outcomes, forks from t* keep the realised answer clearly less than 80% of the time, and the residual sampling share of flip variance at t* is roughly 0.3 or more.
- The hindsight figures (0.35-0.44x tokens in 2611.02278; 14.2% oracle budget in 2610.13570) then overstate what any online rule can reach.
- The reachable frontier from M3 sits at a stated point between today's rules (19-43% saving) and hindsight.
- It replicates on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-9B and the public R1-Distill rollouts.
- Probe within-problem AUROC sits at the ceiling the p_i distribution implies, which would explain the 0.6-0.7 plateau.
- The contribution is the reachable early-exit bound plus a fork-and-vote or lower-temperature-after-formation method that beats the long tail at equal tokens.

**Weaker but publishable outcome: prefix-decided, signal is the problem**
- Residual share below 0.1 at t*, readout rules still miss it, and a fork-supervised probe reaches within-problem AUROC above 0.85 and recovers most of the hindsight saving at under 1 point loss.
- The probe-exit design itself is already occupied, so the within-problem evaluation and the bound would carry the novelty:
  - 2606.13603: probe-based exit at a "commitment boundary", CoT length down "up to 55%".
  - 2603.05488: probe-guided exit, up to 80% on MMLU and 30% on GPQA-Diamond.

A result that only holds pooled across problems, not within problem, is not a paper; 2609.03436 has shown that pooled signals are difficulty proxies.
feasible.blockers:
No kernel work and no training are needed. The blockers are engine fidelity, premise and overlap.

**Engine and method**
1. **Presence penalty breaks forks on Qwen3.5.** vLLM 0.32 applies it to output tokens only (vllm/model_executor/layers/utils.py: `logits -= presence_penalties.unsqueeze(dim=1) * output_mask`). A fork that carries the thinking prefix in the prompt restarts the penalty, so with the model-card setting (presence penalty 1.5) forks are not samples of the base process. Fix: a custom logits processor seeded with the prefix tokens (about half a day), or keep Qwen3-8B as the primary model.
2. **No hidden states from vLLM.** A separate HF pass over the anchors is needed; .venv-hybrid covers it.
3. **Truncation.** 2611.02278 reports 213 of 1,276 hard-set Qwen3.5-9B traces truncated at 32K, with a mean of 7,379 + 8,677 thinking tokens. On disk, Qwen3.5-4B at T=1 hit the 8K cap in 546 of 1,024 samples. Fork tails are long and censored; truncation has to be its own outcome.
4. **Power.** Only problems with mixed outcomes are informative, and they are a small minority on MATH-500, so screening and harder sets are required. AIME sets have 30 problems each.

**Machine**
5. **Cards.** When I checked, only one of cards 1-6 was empty; the rest had 20-33 GB in use. On one card the plan takes about 4 days of wall time, which still fits the week but leaves little slack.
6. **Disk.** /home 38 GB free, /share2 93 GB, / 27 GB. The Thought Anchors data is 19.6 GB compressed and 91 GB as loaded strings, so it must be streamed. Fork outputs are 1-2 GB.

**Premise and overlap (outside this feasibility check, but they change the design)**
7. **Card evidence errors.**
   - "59% of wrong traces also have an early fixed point" is not in 2611.02278. The paper says 59% of thinking tokens in wrong traces come after the fixed point.
   - The accuracy cost of the three-agree rule is 2.4-9.2 points in the abstract and 1.5-9.2 in the body.
   - The anchor "first three agreeing readouts" is mostly a placeholder answer per 2609.09989.
8. **Prior work is closer than the card says.** 2609.03436 runs continuation-versus-restart with a within-problem control and finds problem difficulty explains outcomes, but only for early windows, two small 4-bit models and 4-8 attempts. It explicitly leaves intermediate-answer positions and larger models open. That is the remaining gap.
9. **Unreleased material.** Concise-9B weights have no URL; 2609.09989 code and data are "upon publication"; 2604.06613 releases code (github.com/EdWangLoDaSc/know2say) but not continuation data.

**Search limits**
- The arXiv API returned HTTP 429 throughout, so the prior-answer search rests on Semantic Scholar citation lists and two web searches.
- Paper quotes came through a summarising fetcher, not a raw read.
feasible.follow_on_design_space:
**If a real sampling-decided residual exists at answer formation**
- A reachable-bound standard for exit papers: report savings against the fork-estimated optimal-stopping frontier instead of the hindsight point.
- Fork-and-vote at formation: k short forks sharing the prefix KV instead of one long tail. The cost model uses the measured cache-hit times and block sharing; on hybrid models forks recompute up to 527 tokens because blocks are 528 tokens, which reuses the state-checkpoint residue from D2.
- Lower temperature or greedy decoding after formation, as a zero-cost test of the "tail is a slow resample" reading.
- Engine work: n-way fork admission with copy-on-write blocks in vLLM.
- Speculative decoding by phase: acceptance rate of a sparse self-draft before and after the fixed point (SparseSpec, subspec_v2), since the tail may be cheaper to draft.
- Compression link to residue (a): does weight or KV quantization raise the sampling-decided share, and does that one offline number predict reasoning-length inflation?

**If the answer is prefix-decided**
- A fork-supervised exit head evaluated within problem, run in the engine through a hidden-state hook.
- Denser, cheaper readouts on the cached prefix.
- A placeholder-versus-derived-answer classifier, which targets the specific failure 2609.09989 names.

**If the question decides**
- The direction turns into pre-generation budget routing by question, with early exit as a minor correction. That is a different and more crowded line (2610.13570 puts dynamic routing at 71.4% oracle budget).

verified.question: When sparse attention runs unverified and a reasoning model loses 16.5 points and runs 61% longer although roughly 95% of its tokens agree with dense, is the damage done by the few tokens that fall outside the dense model's nucleus, or by tokens that are individually plausible?

closest_papers.title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Closer than the card credits. Its rule spec_casc_tok is already a plausibility gate: the trusted set is tokens with p(u) >= (1-alpha)*max p, and "draft tokens in the trusted set A_alpha are accepted with probability one". The relaxed-only tokens it admits are 7% of committed draft tokens, "the target's first or second choice (mean rank 0.9, median probability 0.29)". Result: mean length ratio 0.96 over 60 graded cells (median 0.97), mean accuracy loss 0.005, so on average admitting only plausible tokens does not inflate (points to outcome A for EAGLE and small-model drafters). But the same rule gives GPT-OSS-20B on AIME24 a length ratio of 1.48 with accuracy .70 against .767 lossless, and loses two or more points in 22 of 60 cells (points to outcome B on hard reasoning). Appendix C: at Qwen3-8B's recommended sampler (T 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20) mentored_dec, cactus and spec_casc_tok have length ratio 1.01 to 1.04 with accuracy kept. Lossless T=1.2 on GPT-OSS-20B: GSM8K 1.27x longer, accuracy 0.96 vs 0.97; Qwen3-8B barely lengthens (1.02 to 1.04). Appendix F: a per-token guard tuned on eight AIME24 cases cut mean length 13,364 to 10,534 there but moved all 30 cases from 9,270 to 10,363 tokens; a per-token guard "cannot see whether a run will ever close its trace". The paper states its results "do not show why an unlikely token makes a reasoning model think more rather than less". Not covered: no self-speculative, sparse or quantized self-draft; tokens are split by lossless-accept versus relaxed-only, not by nucleus membership; no random-substitution control; no cumulative divergence measure.

closest_papers.title: Revisiting Lossy Verification in Speculative Decoding: Mechanisms, Trade-offs, and Failure Modes
closest_papers.what_it_shows: The card's harvest listed this as not read; it bears directly on the question. It studies truncation-based verification, h(x) = 1{x in A_Theta}: "a draft token is accepted if it lies in A_Theta, and tokens outside this set are rejected" (allowed sets from min-p and eta-sampling). That is the nucleus-gate arm with external drafters. Finding: accuracy falls below the matched truncation-sampling baseline of the target, the gap "grows with task difficulty", "+0.38 pp on GSM8K to +6.67 pp on AIME" (SpecCascade, Figure 1). Table 3 (Llama-3.1-8B + EAGLE-3): MATH 76.16 vs min-p 76.88; typical acceptance 69.84 vs eta-sampling 76.12. Stated cause: the rule produces "a distribution that mirrors the draft model rather than the target distribution", and the effect "is further amplified" under EAGLE-3; its Theorem 1 says the distortion goes to zero as the draft approaches the target. So in-set acceptance of individually plausible tokens is already shown to cost accuracy on hard problems, with a drafter-bias explanation that predicts a small effect for a near-identical self-draft. Not covered: output length is not measured (block efficiency and tokens/s only), no reasoning models, no self or sparse draft. Only the first 100K of 187K characters were read.

closest_papers.title: Nucleus Speculative Decoding: Plausibility-Aware Verification Beyond Exact Distribution
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Rule: "accepts a draft token if it passes the standard test or belongs to the target nucleus" (theta = 0.95, no renormalisation). "over half of the rejected tokens lie inside the target's own nucleus" (52.6% at 0.95); rescued tokens: 94.1% in the target's top five. Accuracy versus lossless SD ranges -1.58 to +4.14 points, +0.40 average, 15 of 30 comparisons up and 14 down, on Qwen3 4B/8B/14B with DSpark and on Nemotron diffusion models with a LoRA self-draft; benchmarks include MATH500 and AIME24/25/26. Confirmed in the body: no per-problem completion length or end-to-end time is reported, only token throughput and tokens per verification. It does not say whether Qwen3 thinking mode was on. No sparse-attention or quantized self-draft.

closest_papers.title: Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention: Closed-Loop Quality Control for Long-Context LLM Decoding (Appendix P)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Source of the anomaly. Appendix P confirmed: R1-Distill-Llama-8B, MATH-500, 200 problems, seed-paired; CVSA-c4 64.0% vs dense 80.5%; M=1 refresh 75.0% (paired CI [+5.5, +16.5]); cap-outs 31 to 13 of 200; length inflation +61% to +20%; residual 5.5 points. The appendix has no token-level analysis: no agreement rate with dense, no dense probability or nucleus membership of the divergent tokens. I did not find the card's "roughly 95% of tokens agree" figure in Appendix P; that number matches first-token acceptance of sparse self-drafts in ASPIRE and S3R (per the harvest notes), not a CVSA measurement. Main text says "Long chain-of-thought reasoning is out of scope". Sampler and token cap for Appendix P were not stated in the part read.

closest_papers.title: A Practical Investigation of Training-free Relaxed Speculative Decoding
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Also listed as not read in the harvest. Thinking-mode AIME24, GPQA, LiveCodeBench with Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen3-32B, Llama-3.1-70B verifiers; rules CACTUS (draft tokens outside the verifier's top-p/top-k support always rejected), mentored-dec, r-fuzzy, spec-casc-opt, ens, spec-cont-dec. Generation length is in its speed-up model; Finding 5: weak drafters lead to longer "rambling" responses. With a strong drafter (Qwen3-8B) trade-offs are sometimes near lossless: "A good drafter under strict rejection != a reliable language model for relaxed rejection." Supports the card's premise that drafter quality governs harm, and predicts a near-identical self-draft is the benign case. No self or sparse draft, no breakdown of which accepted tokens cause the length, no nucleus-only rule tested alone.

closest_papers.title: Reject Only Critical Tokens: Pivot-Aware Speculative Decoding
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Defines harmful (pivot) tokens by downstream effect (expected utility under rollouts drops), not by target probability; about 11% of labelled candidates are pivots (3,657 of 32,619); a classifier on hidden state plus target probability and entropy reaches AUC 0.865, with only a 1e-4 probability guardrail. On AIME24 at sigma 0.7 accuracy falls to 57 against 73. Evidence that probability alone does not identify harmful tokens with a small-model drafter. Qwen3-0.6B/8B only, no self or sparse draft, no length statistics.

closest_papers.title: Quantized Reasoning Models Think They Need to Think Longer, but They Do Not
closest_papers.what_it_shows: For weight quantization, attributes longer reasoning to plausible tokens at uncertain positions: "quantization noise can shift the sampled token toward an overthinking marker" (Wait, But). Per-position KL vs full-precision entropy rho = 0.92 on MATH-500; a logit penalty on 50 markers cuts CoT length 12 to 23% with accuracy kept. This is the outcome-B mechanism (in-support marker tokens) shown for quantization, correlationally. No dense probability or nucleus membership of the divergent tokens, no token-replacement test, no sparse attention.

closest_papers.title: Lost in Rounding: bf16 Recurrent State Makes Hybrid Reasoning Models Think Longer
closest_papers.what_it_shows: A published systematic-versus-random control for a different perturbation: same-width stochastic rounding removes the length increase in four of five affected models, "so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution"; the head octile with the largest teacher-forced KL share (49%) has no detectable length effect. So a strong reader would already predict that the card's arm 4 (random in-nucleus substitutions) inflates less than the systematic sparse error. No token-level divergence analysis, no sparse attention, no verification rule.

closest_papers.title: Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Shows the unverified-sparse inflation is general, not specific to CVSA: Qwen3-8B at a 1,024-token budget, length relative to full KV on AIME25 / MATH-500: TriAttention 1.75x / 1.70x, SeerAttention-R 1.54x / 1.35x, QUEST 1.29x / 1.21x, FASA 1.30x / 1.17x, JSSA 1.07x / 1.09x. Notes "degraded sparse attention can destabilize reasoning trajectories even when the final answer remains correct". No token-level analysis and no verification experiment. Useful for the card's stop rule (arm 2 should reproduce).

closest_papers.title: Calibrated e-CUSUM Decoding for Quantized Reasoning Models: Why Token Log-Probability Is the Wrong Observable for Decoding Monitors
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Not an answer. The title claim is about the model's own log-probability: log p(w_t) + H_t is "a mean-zero martingale by construction under the model's own sampling law" and is silent in a confident loop. It does not measure the full-precision probability or nucleus membership of the quantized model's tokens, and is one model (R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B NF4), 100 GSM8K problems, accuracy 63% to 69% (p = 0.18) at +28% tokens. It does not pre-empt the card's running-divergence budget, which would use the dense target's probabilities.

closest_papers.title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Relevant caveat for the nucleus-gate arm at a truncated sampler: under top-p 0.9, 71% to 100% of repeated units stay locked because the loop token becomes the only candidate left after truncation, while pure sampling locks no position. Loops are made entirely of in-support tokens. No sparse attention, quantization effect, or verification.

closest_papers.title: SSV (2605.19893) and Dustin (2606.24957): sparse verification for speculative decoding
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Both commit tokens judged by a sparse-attention target, which is a lossy sparse path into the output. Neither measures output length, neither uses reasoning models, neither analyses the tokens where sparse and dense verification disagree. Dustin: LongBench average 55.23 vs 55.81 lossless on Qwen2.5-72B at 512 budget. Not an answer.

answered.remaining_gap:
No paper found runs the card's experiment: a sparse-attention self-draft on a reasoning model, committed under a dense-nucleus gate, with length, cap-outs and accuracy measured against dense, plus a control that makes random in-nucleus substitutions at the same rate. Nobody has reported the dense-model probability or nucleus membership of the tokens where sparse and dense attention diverge, and nobody has tested a cumulative-divergence budget against the dense target. That residue is real.

What is already in print narrows it more than the card says, and makes the outcome more predictable:

1. The 'plausible tokens only' intervention has been run with external drafters, twice. In 2610.23818, spec_casc_tok accepts with probability one any draft token with p >= (1-alpha)*max p; the tokens it adds have median target probability 0.29 and mean rank 0.9. Mean length ratio 0.96, mean accuracy loss 0.005, yet GPT-OSS-20B on AIME24 runs 1.48x longer at .70 vs .767. In 2607.26627, accepting any draft token inside the target's min-p / eta set loses accuracy that grows with difficulty (+0.38 pp on GSM8K to +6.67 pp on AIME), explained as the output mirroring the draft inside the allowed set, with a theorem that the distortion vanishes as the draft approaches the target. The card's statement that 2610.23818 has 'no intervention that accepts only in-nucleus tokens' is therefore too strong; the rule uses a relative-probability threshold rather than top-p, but it is the same kind of gate. Length is unmeasured in 2607.26627 and in Nucleus SD.

2. Taken together these predict the mixed result the card's own judge leaned toward: a plausibility gate removes most inflation on easy and medium tasks, a residue remains on hard reasoning, and the residue shrinks as the drafter approaches the target. A sparse self-draft with about 95% first-token agreement is the most favourable drafter, so the likely result is a length ratio between the card's two thresholds (1.05 to 1.15), which the decision rule does not resolve.

3. The systematic-versus-random arm has a published analogue: 2611.12127 shows unbiased rounding of the same size removes the length increase ('mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution'), and 2606.00206 ties quantization inflation to plausible marker tokens at high-entropy positions. An expert would predict arm 4 (random substitutions) inflates less than arm 2.

4. 2610.23818 Appendix F already reports that a per-token guard does not transfer beyond its tuning cases, which is weak prior evidence for outcome B's 'no per-token rule separates harmful from harmless', again only for an EAGLE drafter on GPT-OSS-20B.

What stays untouched and specific to this card: (a) whether sparse-attention error, which comes from missing context rather than a weaker model, behaves like the benign 'draft close to target' case or like a persistent bias that a per-token gate cannot see; this is where CVSA's M=1 result (+20% length with fresh per-step selection) is the unexplained anomaly; (b) the offline measurement of where sparse and dense diverge by dense probability and nucleus membership on reasoning traces; (c) whether a sequence-level log-ratio budget under the dense target predicts or prevents the inflation.

Two card details to correct before use: the '~95% of tokens agree with dense' figure was not found in CVSA Appendix P (it corresponds to first-token acceptance in ASPIRE / S3R), so the premise pairs an accuracy loss from one paper with an agreement rate from others; and the quoted sentence 'A draft token outside the target's top-p/top-k support is rejected regardless of alpha' was not located in the part of 2610.23818 I could read (the equivalent statement about CACTUS is in 2607.08690).

evidence_checks.claim: CVSA App. P: unverified sparse attention on reasoning loses 16.5 points, +61% length; per-step refresh still leaves +20% and a 5.5-point gap (and, in the card's headline, 'roughly 95% of its tokens agree with dense').
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Numbers are exact (arXiv 2611.10634, Appendix P 'Reasoning-length generation'): "on MATH-500 (R1-Distill-Llama-8B, 200 problems, seed-paired sampling) CVSA-c4 reaches 64.0% against dense 80.5% ... refreshing the selection every step (M=1) recovers two-thirds of the gap, to 75.0% ... cap-outs fall from 31 to 13 of 200 problems and generation-length inflation from +61% to +20% above dense. A residual 5.5-point gap remains". Three problems with how the card uses it. (1) The 95% token-agreement figure is not in CVSA at all; CVSA reports no per-token agreement or KL for this run. Per the local harvest notes it comes from ASPIRE 2609.17943 (Qwen3-8B, 7% budget, T=0.7, with verification-driven refresh; not re-read this session), a different model and a different system. In CVSA's M=4 run with no dense refresh the agreement could be far lower, so the headline 'loses 16.5 points although 95% agree' joins two papers. (2) The paper gives no temperature, top-p, token cap or dense cap-out count for this run, so the first experiment cannot 'reproduce CVSA's setting' as stated. (3) The paper's own reading is that "The reuse window, rather than verification, accounts for the larger part of this loss", i.e. stale selection. The coverage identity is an equality on per-step attention-output L2 error; it bounds nothing about the token distribution, so the +20% at M=1 is simply the same unverified effect at smaller size and is not evidence about in-nucleus versus out-of-nucleus tokens. Also 16.5 points is 33 problems against 31 cap-outs: the loss is nearly all non-terminating runs, a heavy tail, not a uniform lengthening.

evidence_checks.claim: Acceptance Is Not Speed: relaxed rules accept 1.34x tokens per round but give 1.54x longer completions; relaxed-only tokens have median target probability 0.01-0.09.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Verified in arXiv 2610.23818 (abstract, section 3.7, Table B2). Scope: the token-probability split is from GPT-OSS-20B + EAGLE-3 only, 15 traced cases per dataset and arm. The card leaves out the other half of the same table, which already bears on its question: "spec_casc_tok admits the fewest extra tokens (7%), and they are the target's first or second choice (mean rank 0.9, median probability 0.29)", and that rule has median lambda 0.97 and is dropped from the timing analysis "because its completions do not grow". So the paper already contains a natural experiment in which admitting only individually plausible tokens does not inflate, while rules admitting tokens of mean target rank 37 to 234 do.

evidence_checks.claim: With a truncated sampler, where out-of-support draft tokens are always rejected, the gentle rules stop inflating.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: The result quote is exact (section 3.3, Appendix C, Table C1; sampler is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20): mentored_dec, cactus and spec_casc_tok "no longer lengthen completions (lambda 1.01 to 1.04)". But the sentence "A draft token outside the target's top-p/top-k support is rejected regardless of alpha" sits in Appendix A's description of CACTUS only; it is not stated as a property of all rules. There is no 'Table A1 note' saying this. And the change is small: at T=1.0 the same pair (Qwen3-8B + EAGLE-3) already had lambda 1.03, 1.04, 0.99 on GSM8K (marked not significant) and 1.05, 1.15, 1.00 on LiveCodeBench in Table 1. So 'stops inflating' is mostly 'was barely inflating on this model'. spec_casc_opt still inflates 1.52x and 1.48x at the truncated sampler, with 87% and 99% of runs at the budget.

evidence_checks.claim: Lossless decoding at T=1.2 inflates GSM8K length 1.27x with accuracy unchanged, although every committed token is in the target's support (used by the card as evidence that individually plausible tokens cause inflation).
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: The number is exact (Appendix C) but it is GPT-OSS-20B only, and the card's reading is the opposite of the paper's. The paper presents it as a control that agrees with the low-probability-token account: "A lossless control agrees: raising the sampling temperature from 1.0 to 1.2, which also commits lower-probability tokens, lengthens GPT-OSS-20B completions by 1.27x on GSM8K and 1.07x on LiveCodeBench". A hotter sampler raises the rate of tokens outside the T=1.0 nucleus, so this does not separate the two hypotheses. The card also omits the next sentence: "Qwen3-8B behaves differently: its completions barely lengthen at T = 1.2 or 1.5 (lambda 1.02 to 1.04 ...)". Qwen3-8B is the card's second model, so its arm 5 is already known to be flat there (caveat: the paper says the 2,048-token GSM8K budget is tight for Qwen3-8B, with 25% of lossless runs at the cap, so some of that flatness may be censoring).

evidence_checks.claim: Nucleus SD accepts every rejected draft token inside the target nucleus, reports accuracy slightly up, measures token throughput not completion length, and has no self-draft.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Quotes verified (arXiv 2610.07822: abstract, 4.1, 4.2); T=1.0, target top-p 1.0, threshold 0.95; completion length is not reported anywhere. Correction: NSD does include a self-speculative setting. The Nemotron runs are "linear self-speculation" (draft pass with LoRA enabled, target pass with adapters disabled, 32-token blocks). It is not a sparse or quantized self-draft, but 'no self-draft' is wrong. NSD also reports that "86.65% of additional acceptances lie in the nucleus core" and 94.1% rank in the target's top five, and on MATH500/AIME25 with Qwen3.5-4B MTP accuracy is 92.73 vs 92.33 and 35.56 vs 34.44. If the gate produced many cap-outs, accuracy would have dropped; the token budget is not stated, so this is indirect.

evidence_checks.claim: The drafter matters: standalone language-model drafters inflate least; a sparse self-draft was not tested.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Quote verified (2610.23818, section 3.3). The paper goes further, in the direction of the card's own expert prediction: "Drafters that sample close to the target inflate little" and "the standalone Qwen3 drafters lengthen completions significantly in none of their 60 cells", even under the loosest relaxed rules. A sparse-attention copy of the target is closer to the target than Qwen3-1.7B is. No sparse, quantized or layer-skip self-draft appears in the paper.

evidence_checks.claim: Weight quantization and KV eviction also lengthen reasoning, sometimes with accuracy kept.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Abstracts verified: 2606.25519 "INT4/INT3 quantization can preserve accuracy but increase reasoning-token usage"; 2512.12008 "eviction strategies at low budgets can produce longer reasoning traces". Neither gives a mechanism or a per-token analysis. Background only; it does not bear on in-nucleus versus out-of-nucleus.

evidence_checks.claim: No paper has tried a per-token intervention against length inflation or explained it (prior-answer search).
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: No paper found that applies a nucleus gate to a sparse self-draft and reports length (arXiv API and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited this session; two WebSearch queries found nothing closer). But 2610.23818 Appendix F did try per-token guards: an agent-searched guard that forces lossless verification at chosen positions "on all 30 cases ... moved the mean from 9 270 to 10 363 tokens", i.e. did not help, and the authors conclude "A guard judges one draft token at a time and cannot see whether a run will ever close its trace". The paper states the open part plainly: "They do not show why an unlikely token makes a reasoning model think more rather than less." 2607.11317 (e-CUSUM monitor for quantized reasoning models, abstract read) already argues that token log-probability is a poor health signal and that non-termination, not looping, dominates; that is close to the card's outcome-B design.

premise.predicted_answer: Mostly the out-of-nucleus (low dense-probability) tokens. I would bet about 3:1 that a dense-nucleus gate on a sparse self-draft removes at least two-thirds of the inflation and puts accuracy inside the paired CI of dense, and about 5:1 against the card's outcome B (gated length ratio >= 1.15). On Qwen3-8B I would bet 4:1 or better on a gated ratio <= 1.05, because that model barely lengthens even at T=1.5 and under the gentle relaxed rules. On R1-Distill-Llama-8B I expect the gated arm at roughly 1.03-1.10, which falls in the undecided band between the card's two thresholds, so the planned experiment most likely returns 'mostly A with a small residual' and settles neither design. Reasons: (1) in 2610.23818 the one rule that admits only top-ranked tokens (spec_casc_tok, mean rank 0.9, median p 0.29) does not inflate while rules admitting rank 37-234 tokens do; (2) drafters close to the target (standalone Qwen3) inflate in none of 60 cells; (3) NSD's gate keeps MATH500/AIME accuracy; (4) CVSA's loss is almost entirely cap-outs driven by a stale reuse window, the kind of gross error a dense gate catches. The residual I cannot rule out is the systematic-bias path: a 0.95 nucleus still admits a token dense rates at 0.03 that the sparse draft rates at 0.3, repeatedly at the same kind of decision.
premise.strongest_argument_it_is_boring: The 'contradiction' is assembled from misread evidence, and once it is read correctly every source points the same way. The three results the card says 'point the other way' do not: (a) the T=1.2 control is offered by its own authors as support for the low-probability-token account ('also commits lower-probability tokens'), it raises the out-of-nucleus rate rather than holding it fixed, it is GPT-OSS-20B only, and Qwen3-8B, the card's second model, is flat at T=1.2 and 1.5; (b) CVSA at M=1 is still ungated sparse sampling, and the coverage identity bounds attention-output error, not the token distribution, so its +20% says nothing about which tokens do the damage; (c) the systematic-bias argument has no data behind it. The headline '95% of tokens agree' is imported from a different paper, model and system (ASPIRE, with dense refresh), so the puzzle 'large damage despite 95% agreement' may not exist in CVSA's run at all. Meanwhile the existing data already answer the dichotomy for other drafters: admitting only target-top-ranked tokens does not inflate (spec_casc_tok), closer drafters inflate less, and a sparse self-draft is the closest drafter there is. So this is 'does a published result (NSD's nucleus gate, 2610.23818's low-probability account) carry over to drafter X', the shape the first search was faulted for, and the card's own expert and judge both predict the same middling answer. The payoff is also small: outcome A is NSD applied to SparseSpec, worth at most about 1.33x in tokens per verification round by the card's own arithmetic (9.9 to 13.5 accepted at k=16) and less in wall-clock because the sparse draft pass is not free; outcome B's 'running divergence budget' is close to the e-CUSUM monitor of 2607.11317, and 2610.23818 App. F already reports that per-token guards fail to shorten runs. Finally, the gate arm needs the dense forward at every step, so it is a verification rule, not a test of unverified sparse attention.
premise.sharpened_question: What survives is not 'in-nucleus or out-of-nucleus' but 'is length inflation a function of per-token divergence alone, or of what context was removed'. Concretely: at a matched per-token divergence profile from dense (same rate of substituted tokens and same distribution of their dense probability and rank), does a sparse-attention self-draft lengthen a reasoning trace more than (i) random substitutions drawn to the same profile and (ii) a hotter lossless sampler tuned to the same profile? If the three match, length inflation is predicted by one offline number (cumulative excess surprisal under dense) and a token-level gate or budget is enough for any lossy method; if sparse is worse at matched divergence, the harm is tied to losing the model's own earlier derivations and the fix is in the selector (what must stay visible), not in the acceptance rule. This connects to residue (a) of the first search. It should be run on a model whose length is known to respond to low-probability tokens (R1-Distill-Llama-8B, or GPT-OSS-20B, which inflates 1.27x at T=1.2), not Qwen3-8B, which is flat. A second unexplained and grounded anomaly from the same paper is worth stating separately: why GPT-OSS-20B inflates 1.27x at T=1.2 and 3.94x at T=1.5 while Qwen3-8B stays at 1.02-1.04 (after ruling out the 2,048-token cap as the cause), i.e. what property of a model sets its length sensitivity to unlikely tokens. Cheap first step before any closed-loop build: replay ungated sparse traces teacher-forced under dense and check whether cap-out runs are preceded by out-of-nucleus tokens or by none; if nearly every sparse token in the cap-out runs is inside the dense nucleus, the systematic-bias path is real and the question is worth the full harness; if not, stop.
