verified.question: A sparse-KV self-draft whose selection is fresh is still rejected on about 5% of tokens: are those the tokens where the dense target is itself close to undecided (so any small perturbation loses them), or tokens where one needed KV entry was missing and the draft is confidently wrong?

closest_papers.title: Vegas: Self-Speculative Decoding with Verification-Guided Sparse Attention
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Closest direct evidence, and the card misses it. Section 3.2 / Figure 5 plots the 'Distribution of acceptance probability of rejected tokens' for a sparse-KV self-draft (7% of KV, LongBench-v2, sampling) and states: 'Many rejected tokens are sampled from a distribution that closely matches the one predicted by full attention' and 'many draft tokens possessing a high acceptance probability are rejected due to probabilistic sampling'. So under sampling a published figure already says a large share of rejections are near-miss, not confidently wrong. It is qualitative in the text (no share given), has no target entropy or margin, no coverage feature, no greedy case. Also reports that the accepted count versus budget 'rises initially and then reaches a relatively stable level'.

closest_papers.title: Long-Context Drafting Does Not Require Long-Context Drafters
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Measures the dense target against the same target on a hard recency window (a sparse self-draft with window selection, not attention top-K), per position, Qwen2.5-7B at 32k, 1750 positions (Section 6.5, Appendices F and I, read from the PDF). 'The mean gap ... falls from 0.2195 at W = 128 to 0.0444 at W = 16384, the greedy flip rate from 0.247 to 0.063, and at the deployed W = 2048 truncation changes the target's greedy token at 12.1% of positions.' By entropy tier at W = 2048: 'greedy flip rates 0.146 and 0.058' on high-entropy versus low-entropy documents (document-level third-party labels, called preliminary). '590 of the 1347 positions that cross below τ = 0.05 at some window later return above it, or 43.8%'. Two consequences: flips are more frequent where the target is more uncertain (document level), and the greedy flip rate is above mean TV at every window, so near-equal T=0 and T=1 acceptance is what this data shows rather than an anomaly. No per-token margin, no coverage, no confident-wrong measure, no attention-based selection.

closest_papers.title: TriForce: Lossless Acceleration of Long Sequence Generation with Hierarchical Speculative Decoding
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Oracle selection has already been measured in aggregate: 'Figure 3(b) demonstrates that utilizing only 1K tokens could theoretically achieve a 97.6% acceptance rate with Top-K selection method ... practical implementations like H2O and StreamingLLM ... achieving over 90.5% acceptance rates with 1K KV cache budget.' So about 2.4% of tokens are lost even with the token's own top-K, and practical selectors lose several points more. Also 'the acceptance rate rises with the cache budget up to 4K, then plateaus towards 1.0'. No per-token attribution. Note for the card: the Table 2 parenthesised number is described only as the average acceptance rate of TriForce's hierarchical drafting; the paper does not name which draft-target pair it is, so reading it as the sparse-KV self-draft rate is an assumption.

closest_papers.title: Accelerating Large-Scale Reasoning Model Inference with Sparse Self-Speculative Decoding (SparseSpec)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Figure 3 uses 'self-speculation with oracle Top-K attention' as an upper bound and says 'MagicDec fails to approach the acceptance rate of the oracle top-k attention'. Section 5.4: 'We set the sparsity ratio to 0.05, as performance saturates with further increases in selected tokens.' Aggregate only; no entropy, margin, coverage or per-token analysis; temperature fixed at 0.65.

closest_papers.title: A Sparse Glimpse of the Whole: Train-Free Self-Speculative Decoding (SparseSpec-L)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Only per-token predictor in the sparse self-draft papers, and it is draft-side: 'negative draft entropy obtains an acceptance AUC of 0.638 on RULER QA1. Tokens in the low-entropy bin are accepted at 86.3%, compared with 62.1% in the high-entropy bin.' Target entropy, margin and coverage do not appear; no split of rejections by cause.

closest_papers.title: Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention: Closed-Loop Quality Control for Long-Context LLM Decoding (CVSA)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Coverage is tied by an exact identity to the attention-output vector error, and failures are intermittent: 'intermittent cells failing on 5 – 80 % of steps account for 86.4 %, and the set of failing heads overlaps by a Jaccard index of only 0.33 between consecutive steps'. Both halves of the page were read: nothing links coverage to argmax flips, TV/KL of the next-token distribution, target entropy or margin, or speculative acceptance.

closest_papers.title: Dustin: Draft-Augmented Sparse Verification for Efficient Long-Context Generation with Speculative Decoding
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Appendix B reports that the attention recovery rate (share of attention mass kept by the selected KV) correlates with output KL at -0.9490 (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) and -0.8079 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), computed per sampled KV subset and averaged over decoding steps. This is aggregate evidence that coverage drives output error, but it is not per token and not conditioned on the target's margin. Only the first 100K characters were read.

closest_papers.title: S3R: Fast and Faithful RL Rollouts via Self-Sparse Speculative Decoding
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Body and appendices read. Budget sweep ('Increasing s from 0.05 to 0.50 raises acceptance from 80.4% to 96.7%') and position decay ('acceptance falls from 95.8% for the first proposed token to 67.9% for the sixth'). Appendix D.2 only names the two candidate causes without separating them: 'Acceptance can still vary with the sparse approximation and the target distribution'. No per-token TV/KL, no oracle selection, no coverage analysis.

closest_papers.title: ASPIRE: Asynchronous Batched Self-Speculative Decoding for Long-Context LLM Inference
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Measures attention-mass recall of selected pages against an oracle ('The oracle uses the target token/layer's own attention map to select the top-100 pages') and how recall decays with token lag, but relates recall to acceptance only through aggregate ablations. No entropy, margin, temperature sweep or per-token cause analysis.

closest_papers.title: EfficientRollout: System-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding for RL Rollouts
closest_papers.what_it_shows: The r = -0.99 entropy correlation is across RL training steps, not across tokens: Fig. 2(c) caption 'Inverse correlation between target-policy entropy and quantized-drafter first-token acceptance over steps'; Appendix C gives 'Pearson correlations ranging from -0.96 to -0.99'. answered.remaining_gap:
No paper found takes a sparse-KV self-draft with fresh selection and attributes its per-token rejections jointly to target-side features (entropy, top-2 margin) and draft-side retrieval features (per-head coverage), nor reports how confident the draft is at rejected positions, nor compares the greedy and T=1 rejection sets.

What is already in print narrows the question more than the card admits:
- Under sampling, Vegas Figure 5 already states that many rejected tokens come from a draft distribution that closely matches full attention (near-miss rejections). The card does not cite this.
- Oracle top-K selection still loses about 2.4% of tokens (TriForce, 97.6% at 1K), against over 90.5% for practical selectors. So the size of the selector gap is known in aggregate.
- For a recency-window self-draft, 2610.20865 gives per-position TV and greedy flip rates and shows flips are 2.5 times more frequent on high-entropy documents (0.146 against 0.058). Its greedy flip rate is above mean TV at every window, which removes most of the card's 'greedy should be well above sampling' anomaly.
- Coverage predicts output KL in aggregate (Dustin, -0.95 / -0.81) and equals attention-output error exactly (CVSA).

An expert can assemble these into the card's own 'mixed, mostly target-side with a retrieval-miss tail' prediction, so the result is less surprising than claimed. The untouched residue is the quantitative per-token decomposition on reasoning traces with attention-based top-K selection: AUC of target-only versus coverage-only features, the confident-wrong share, and the oracle versus previous-step gap at equal budget broken down by target margin.

evidence_checks.claim: ASPIRE (2609.17943): zero-staleness 7% sparse draft is accepted ~95%; with per-step refresh the decay matches a constant 5% per-token loss.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Quote is in Appendix D: "At γ=1 both variants achieve near-identical acceptance (∼95%), since the context has not yet gone stale" and 60.3% vs 76.6% at γ=10. Setting: Qwen3-8B, LB[16k-18k] (LongBench long-context, not reasoning traces), B=24, ρ=7%. The appendix does not define the acceptance metric for that figure (Algorithm 1 uses a/min(a+1,d), tables use an average over verification rounds), and temperature is not stated there. So the 'constant 5% per token' reading is the card's arithmetic on an undefined metric. 'With refresh' is a single intra-draft refresh layer, not a full fresh selection.

evidence_checks.claim: S3R (2610.13202): same ~95% first-position number at 5% budget and T=1.0; ten times the budget removes most of the loss.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Both quotes are present. "For Qwen3-8B at step 20, acceptance falls from 95.8% for the first proposed token to 67.9% for the sixth" (Appendix E.2; s=0.05 and T=1.0 come from Appendix C.2; RL policy on DAPO-MATH-17k). The sweep "Increasing s from 0.05 to 0.50 raises acceptance from 80.4% to 96.7%" is at a frozen step-60 checkpoint with k=6, and the method "holds the historical selection fixed" across the k steps. So 80.4% is an all-position figure that includes staleness; the paper does not show that the first-position (fresh) 4-5% loss shrinks with budget. It also gives no per-position figure at s=0.50.

evidence_checks.claim: SparseSpec (2512.01278) reports the opposite about budget: more selected tokens stop helping at 5%.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Quotes are present. 6.16 of 8 is averaged "across different models and datasets" at temperature 0.65, bonus token not counted. The saturation sentence refers to Figure 12 (right), acceptance vs budget ratio at k=8 averaged over models and datasets; the text gives no numbers or sweep range. It is a justification of a default, as is S3R's own "supporting our default s = 0.05". Different temperature (0.65 vs 1.0), pretrained reasoning models vs a mid-RL exploring policy, different draft length. Not a contradiction; both readings of the card's question also predict that acceptance rises with budget, so the sweep does not discriminate between them.

evidence_checks.claim: TriForce (2404.11912) Table 2: sparse-KV self-draft acceptance is almost the same under greedy and T=1 sampling, which fits a fixed subset of grossly wrong positions rather than small noise.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Table numbers are correct (0.9234 / 0.9137 / 0.9004 / 0.8902; naive 68M draft 0.4649 -> 0.2664). The inference drawn from them does not hold. (1) The paper never states top-p; the public code (Infini-AI-Lab/TriForce, utils/sampling.py and test/on_chip.py) defaults to top_p=0.9 and the example command passes --top_p 0.9, so the T=1.0 row is probably nucleus sampling, which collapses peaked positions to near-greedy. (2) The metric is accepted_count/draft_count over a whole round (the script prints "average acceptance rate (NOT per token)"), with a retrieval cache reused across steps, so it is neither fresh-selection nor per-token. (3) Llama2-7B-128K, PG-19, 122K prompt, 256 generated tokens: book continuation, not reasoning. (4) First principles: for small logit perturbations the argmax-flip probability and E[TV] are equal to first order (both ~ density of near-ties times mean perturbation). A CPU toy I ran (target calibrated to mean top-prob 0.86, median 0.98) gave greedy 0.944 vs T=1 sampling 0.951 under purely diffuse noise, and 0.946 vs 0.953 under a 5% gross-miss model: indistinguishable. Greedy much higher than sampling is the signature of a large divergence (the 68M draft), not of small noise. The 'anomaly' is not one.

It says nothing per token and nothing about sparse drafts, so it does not conflict with the SparseSpec-L number.

evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Quote present: "negative draft entropy obtains an acceptance AUC of 0.638 on RULER QA1. Tokens in the low-entropy bin are accepted at 86.3%, compared with 62.1% in the high-entropy bin." Model, temperature, draft length and sparsity are not stated for this check; the index is refreshed only after verification, so staleness is mixed in; RULER QA1 is a long-context retrieval task, not a reasoning trace. If verification is stochastic, accept/reject is a Bernoulli draw and even a perfect TV predictor has a low AUC ceiling (two equal bins with TV 0.1 and 0.4 give 0.70), so 0.638 does not show the draft is confidently wrong. No target-entropy, margin or coverage analysis in the paper.

evidence_checks.claim: When Is a Draft Accepted? (2606.30265): most target positions are sharply peaked (mean top-prob ~0.85-0.87, median ~0.97-0.99).

evidence_checks.claim: CVSA (2611.10634): coverage failures are intermittent and move between heads from step to step.

It is a two-sample Llama-3.1-8B HotpotQA trace with fresh selection every step; failing means coverage below τ=0.90 at 5% budget. CVSA is not speculative decoding and reports no token-level outcome (no agreement, KL, margin or entropy analysis), so it does not bear on which tokens get rejected.

premise.predicted_answer: Mixed, and not a real either/or. Rejection probability is target sensitivity times draft logit error, so both factors always show up. On reasoning traces with fresh previous-step top-K at 5%: rejections sit overwhelmingly at low-margin target positions (target margin AUC about 0.8-0.9 under greedy), coverage features add a few points (0.02-0.08), same-step oracle selection cuts the rejection rate by roughly a third to a half, and a minority of rejections (my guess 10-30%) are confident-wrong retrieval misses. On retrieval-style long-context tasks (RULER-like) the miss share is larger. I would bet about 3:1 that the result lands between the card's A and B thresholds or trips both at once (target-only AUC >= 0.85 and oracle halving rejection are not mutually exclusive). The size of the confident-wrong tail is the only part I cannot call.
premise.strongest_argument_it_is_boring:
The card's dichotomy is not a dichotomy, and its main anomaly dissolves.

1. Under speculative sampling the per-token rejection probability is TV(p,q); under greedy it is an argmax flip. To first order both equal (how close the target is to a tie) times (how large the draft's logit error is). 'Target undecided' answers where rejections fall; 'missing entry' answers how big the error is. Both can be true together, and outcome A's design conclusion ('selectors have little headroom') does not follow from A: if the error is diffuse, halving it still halves rejections.

2. The headline evidence (TriForce greedy 0.9234 vs T=1.0 0.9004) is what both hypotheses predict. For small perturbations flip rate and mean TV are equal to first order; my toy gave 0.944 vs 0.951 for diffuse noise and 0.946 vs 0.953 for gross misses. TriForce's code also defaults to top-p 0.9 and reports a whole-round, stale-cache acceptance on PG-19, so the table is not a fresh, per-token, pure-sampling measurement anyway.

3. The other 'conflicts' compare different things: S3R's budget sweep is an all-position figure with a selection held fixed over six steps at T=1 on an exploring RL policy, SparseSpec's 'saturates' is an unquantified default-setting remark at T=0.65; r=-0.99 is an across-training-steps correlation for a quantized draft, AUC 0.638 is per token for draft entropy on a retrieval task with staleness and possibly stochastic verification.

4. The answer follows from known results: rejections at high-entropy target positions are documented for every drafter family (SpecDec++-style stopping heads, EfficientRollout and S3R entropy trends, the margin theory in 2606.30265), and TriForce already reports that oracle top-K reaches 97.6% where practical selectors reach about 90.5%, so selection error is known to be a large share of the loss.

5. Both designs largely exist: an entropy-driven draft-length controller ships in SparseSpec-L (and helps 17% on NIAH, nothing on InfiniteBench); a per-head coverage gate is CVSA. The experiment would choose which to port, not produce a new mechanism. And controller A cannot see target entropy at draft time, only draft entropy.

6. The fresh-selection 5% is the smaller part of the practical loss: S3R goes from 95.8% at position 1 to 67.9% at position 6. Explaining the first-position residue leaves the window decay untouched.
premise.sharpened_question:
Measure the error, not the accept/reject outcome. For a fresh sparse-KV self-draft on reasoning traces, once target sensitivity is divided out, is the draft's per-position logit error roughly constant (diffuse truncation error that shrinks smoothly with budget and is about the same under same-step oracle top-K), or heavy-tailed (a few steps where attention moves to entries outside the previous step's top-K and the draft is confidently wrong)? And if heavy-tailed, is that tail visible at draft time from a cheap coverage estimate (CVSA's log-sum-exp mass) where draft entropy is blind to it?

Concretely: per position log TV(p,q) and logit-error norm, target margin, draft top-prob, per-head coverage; compare lagged vs same-step oracle selection at equal budget; report the share of total TV in the worst 5% of positions after conditioning on target margin, and the draft's top-prob on rejected positions. Heavy-tailed and coverage-visible supports a coverage-triggered early verify; diffuse means only budget or a cheaper draft helps and selector work has no cheap win.

This is narrower than the card and closer to a two-day diagnostic than a headline question. It is not answered in the eight sources or in two web searches (no paper found that decomposes sparse-draft rejections or links coverage to token outcomes; the arXiv API was rate-limited, so the prior-answer search is thin). The outcome is only moderately uncertain: I lean heavy-tailed under lagged selection, diffuse under oracle.

feasible.first_week_experiment:
Offline teacher-forced two-stream replay in plain PyTorch, one card.

Mechanics. Run the whole trace in parallel, not as a decode loop. Stream 0 is dense. Each sparse stream takes its queries from its own hidden states but reads K/V from stream 0 for all earlier positions (its own K/V only on the diagonal). That is exactly the fresh first-draft-token condition. All selector and budget variants go in one batch, with query positions chunked at about 512 (32 heads x 512 x 8192 fp32 scores is about 0.5 GB per stream). Check first that a sparse stream at 100% budget reproduces dense logits to fp32 noise.

Data and models.
- Day 1-2: Qwen3-4B in fp32 on the 76 existing traces, first 8K generated tokens each (about 550K positions).
- Day 3: Qwen3-8B (the SparseSpec / Vegas model). Generate 200 thinking traces (AIME24/25, MATH-500 level 5, LiveCodeBench) at T=0.6, about 1.2M tokens, then replay.
- Day 6-7 if alive: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B as a second family.

Variants. Budgets 2 / 5 / 10 / 25 / 50%, always keeping 4 sink tokens and a recent window. Selectors:
- (a) own-query oracle top-K per head (truncation-only ceiling);
- (b) oracle with one shared set per layer;
- (c) previous-step dense top-K (PillarAttn at zero staleness), plus lags 2 / 4 / 8;
- (d) recent window only;
- (e) random-K plus recent.

Logged per position (keep top-64 logits of each stream, not the full vocabulary).
- TV(p,q) and argmax flip at T=0, at T=0.6 with top-p 0.95 / top-k 20, and at T=1.0.
- Target top-1 probability, entropy, top-2 logit margin m; draft entropy.
- delta = the change the draft causes in the top-1 minus runner-up logit gap.
- Per-(layer, KV group) coverage and attention-output error.

The card's test (AUC of target-only vs coverage-only features) will almost certainly land between its own thresholds, because rejection is roughly perturbation size divided by margin and both families will predict. Use three sharper tests instead.
1. Exchangeability. Shuffle delta across positions within a trace and recompute the rejection set. If the rate and the set match the real ones, the perturbation is position-independent and the target decides. If real rejection is well above shuffled, misses are concentrated or correlated with low margin.
2. Matched other perturbations. Compare the rejected set with (i) the dense-vs-dense bf16 kernel-noise set, (ii) Gaussian noise on the final hidden state at equal norm, (iii) a 4-bit weight-quantized copy tuned to equal aggregate acceptance. Report rank correlation of per-position TV and Jaccard of the flip sets.
3. Single-entry restoration. For about 2,000 rejected positions, add back the j = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 highest-mass missed entries, in all heads and then only in the worst-covered (layer, head). Record the smallest j that restores acceptance.

Also report: a 2D histogram of target top-1 probability against draft top-1 probability over rejection mass (share in the cell where both are above 0.9 and the argmax differs); the distribution of min(1, p/q) for sampled rejections, to compare with Vegas Fig. 5; first-token acceptance at T=0 vs T=1 per selector, to see whether TriForce's 0.9234 vs 0.9004 pattern exists on reasoning traces at all.

Controls: fp32 vs bf16; dense-vs-dense floor; split by thinking vs answer segment and by position in trace; bootstrap over problems.

Cost: about 2 minutes per 8K trace for 12 streams on an A6000 (eager attention plus top-K over 36 layers), about 10 hours for all 276 traces.
feasible.result_that_kills_it:
Any one of these by day 3, on Qwen3-4B with the existing traces, ends it as a research question. I put the combined chance at more than half.

1. The premise does not reproduce offline. With previous-step selection at 5% budget and dense K/V, first-token rejection on reasoning traces is about 1-2%, at or near the dense-vs-dense bf16 floor (0-2% argmax disagreement in /home/ryankert_l/kv-fetch/kv-fetch/results/reasoning/e3_checks/logits.txt). Then the 5% reported by systems comes from staleness, shared sets and bf16, which ASPIRE and Vegas already attribute, and there is nothing left to decompose.

2. The expected mixed answer. Shuffled delta reproduces at least 80% of the real rejection rate, per-position TV under the sparse draft correlates at about 0.8 or more with TV under matched Gaussian or quantization noise, and under 10% of rejection mass sits in the cell where target and draft are both above 0.9 and disagree. That is the card's own expert prediction and the judge's, and the design it implies (set draft length from entropy) is already what SparseSpec-L and SpecDec++ do.

3. The anomaly is a dataset artifact. On reasoning traces greedy acceptance is clearly above T=1 acceptance (for example 98% vs 94%). TriForce's near-equal 0.9234 / 0.9004 is then explained by PG-19 prose, 256 generated tokens and chunk retrieval, and the card's main reason for uncertainty goes away.

Three things I read in this session already weaken the card.
- TriForce (arXiv 2404.11912, https://arxiv.org/html/2404.11912) Table 1, PG-19, 120K context, 4K budget: "Top-K (Ref.)" 0.9921 against "Retrieval" 0.9649. Oracle selection already cuts rejection from 3.5% to 0.8% in that setting, so the card's rule "decide B if oracle selection halves rejection" is met in print for long-context prose.
- Vegas (arXiv 2602.07223, ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/html/2602.07223) Fig. 5: "Many rejected tokens are sampled from a distribution that closely matches the one predicted by full attention", "rejected due to probabilistic sampling". That is a third category the card omits (near-match lost on the random draw) and it points away from confident-wrong. The card does not cite this figure.
- CVSA (arXiv 2611.10634, https://arxiv.org/html/2611.10634) already builds outcome B's design outside speculative decoding: coverage as the acceptance test, recovery of only the failing heads, and an offline per-(layer, head) budget control (b = 5% + r x 15%) that did not beat a uniform budget at matched read (41.03 vs 41.19 average).
feasible.result_that_makes_it_a_paper:
A structured result that neither expert reading predicts, holding on both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B and on math and code. Any of the following would do.

1. Confident-wrong is real and repairable. At least 30% of rejection mass at 5% budget comes from positions where target and draft are both above 0.9 and disagree; these are not the positions that kernel, Gaussian or quantization noise flips (Jaccard under 0.2); and restoring 4 or fewer entries in one (layer, head) recovers acceptance for most of them. That gives a per-token repair rule and says how the missing entry could be recognised before verification. It needs a description of what the missed entries are (for example operand or definition tokens far back in the chain).

2. Fragile positions are universal. The same roughly 5% of positions are lost under sparse KV, weight quantization, KV quantization and kernel noise (rank correlation about 0.9), and a target-side quantity computed offline (margin over a local sensitivity) predicts them with AUC of at least 0.9. That is one perturbation-agnostic acceptance law, and it would settle residue (a) from the first search. It would also explain why selector papers saturate at 5% and why S3R still gains from 5% to 50% budget (the gain should then follow the delta distribution's tail).

3. Coupling. Low-margin positions are also the positions with diffuse, long-range attention, so real rejection is well above the shuffled-delta rate (1.5x or more). Then neither "the target decides" nor "the selector decides" holds; a draft-length or budget controller should key on a cheap attention-shape signal from the last verification pass, and that controller beats draft entropy (SparseSpec-L's AUC 0.638) as an acceptance predictor.

In each case the paper needs a week-2 online confirmation in /home/ryankert_l/SparseSpec/serve: the controller or repair rule raises accepted tokens per verification at equal draft cost on Qwen3-8B.
feasible.blockers:
No hard blocker. In order of weight:

1. The question's dichotomy is not well posed. Rejection depends on perturbation size relative to margin, so "target-undecided vs missing entry" will not separate by AUC of two feature families; the card's thresholds leave a wide middle where week 1 is inconclusive. The experiment has to be the counterfactual version (shuffle, matched noise, restoration), and Vegas Fig. 5 adds a third bucket (near-match lost on the sampling draw) that must be accounted for.

2. Numeric floor. bf16 kernel noise already flips 0-2% of argmaxes on Qwen3-4B (own data). Run fp32 on the 4B model; Qwen3-8B in fp32 needs about 32 GB of weights, so the replay must be chunked carefully on a 48 GB card, or run bf16 with the floor subtracted.

3. New code. The existing SparseEngine is page-granular, one set per layer, and writes sparse K/V. Token-level per-head selection over dense K/V is a new parallel replay, 1-2 days including the 100%-budget equality check.

4. Offline first-token acceptance is not the systems' number. They report chain acceptance with staleness, shared sets and bonus tokens. An online cross-check in SparseSpec serve is possible on A6000 only with `--vanilla-attn` and without CUDA graphs, and that code has no per-position acceptance logging yet.

5. Disk. /home has 38 GB free and is at 100% use. Per-(layer, head) coverage for every position and stream would be about 60 GB; store per-(layer, KV group) values in fp16 or uint8 (about 8 GB) and top-64 logits only, and write to /share1 (372 GB free) or /share3 (105 GB free), not /home.

6. GPUs. When I looked, one card (index 5) was fully idle and one (index 4) lightly used; the rest were busy. The experiment needs one card, so this only slows the controls.

7. Literature search limits. The arXiv API and Semantic Scholar both returned HTTP 429 in this session, so I could not rerun the "already answered" search. I confirmed that the cited papers exist and read the relevant passages of TriForce, Vegas, CVSA, SparseSpec-L and 2606.30265 via arxiv.org HTML. I used one WebSearch.

8. Audience. Even the best outcome serves sparse-KV self-speculation only, a narrow line with four or more 2026 systems already in it (Vegas, ASPIRE, S3R, SparseSpec-L).
feasible.follow_on_design_space:
Only if one of the three paper outcomes holds.

If misses are few-entry and repairable (outcome 1):
- A miss detector that runs before verification: a per-head coverage proxy from the page-score log-sum-exp, as CVSA computes, used as the draft-length controller inside SparseSpec in place of draft entropy.
- Small per-head "rescue" lists refreshed from verification.
- A FlashInfer draft kernel with per-head variable budgets or a two-level cascade (shared set plus a per-head delta). This reuses the cascade kernel in /home/ryankert_l/subspec_v2.
- Per-head budgets are a weak bet as a static allocation: CVSA's offline per-head budget did not beat uniform, so it would have to be dynamic.

If fragile positions are universal (outcome 2):
- A perturbation-agnostic acceptance predictor from target-side margin and sensitivity, taken from the last verification pass.
- With it: draft-length scheduling that works for any self-draft (sparse KV, quantized weights, KV-quantized, layer-skip); stacking cheap drafts until the predicted TV budget is spent; a principled floor on what a better selector can buy, so the selector can be the cheapest page-granular one that vLLM's paged kernels support unchanged.
- It links directly to the open residue about one offline quantity predicting reasoning-length inflation across weight quantization, KV quantization and eviction.

If margin and attention diffuseness are coupled (outcome 3):
- An attention-shape trigger (entropy or coverage of the last verified token's attention) that raises the budget or shortens the draft only at decision points.
- Per-request asynchronous scheduling as in ASPIRE, driven by that signal instead of running acceptance averages.
- A check of whether the same decision points are where lossy sparse decoding goes wrong; kv-fetch E3 has the accuracy side on disk (/home/ryankert_l/kv-fetch/kv-fetch/results/e3_explore.json).

In every case the natural second axis is hybrid GDN + attention models (Qwen3.5), where fewer attention layers carry all retrieval and the miss / margin split may differ. /home/ryankert_l/kv-fetch/kv-fetch/kvfetch/sparse_decode.py already supports those models.

verified.question: When a lossy method (weight quantization, KV quantization, KV eviction or sparse attention, bf16 state rounding) makes a reasoning model think longer, is the cause the persistent, systematic same-direction part of the error (removable by unbiased/stochastic rounding, a bias correction, or randomising the error at equal size) or the per-step size of the error whatever its direction?

closest_papers.title: Lost in Rounding: bf16 Recurrent State Makes Hybrid Reasoning Models Think Longer
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Answers the bias-versus-size question for recurrent state only. Same-width stochastic rounding of the state brings the length ratio back to about x0.99-x1.05 (e.g. Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 x0.991, caps 1 -> 31 -> 0; Qwen3.5-9B x1.031, caps 118 -> 223 -> 111). Setup says "All weights and activations are bf16; only the recurrent state dtype changes between arms." No weight-quantization arm, no KV arm, no Gaussian-noise arm, no bias-correction arm, and the limitations do not mention weights or KV. Zero citations on Semantic Scholar as of today.

closest_papers.title: RATIO: Reasoning Analysis and Token-level Inference Optimization for Quantized Reasoning Models
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Closest partial evidence for the weight case, and not on the card. It measures signed per-token shifts (delta = log pQ - log pF), keeps hesitation tokens ("Wait", "But", "Hmm", "perhaps", "maybe") with "positive shifts in both models" (AWQ and GPTQ, 3-bit, g128), and subtracts a per-token penalty: CoT length falls 51.34% (AWQ-W3) and 25.66% (GPTQ-W3) on Qwen-1.5B. So a same-sign output-level shift exists across two quantizers and removing it shortens thinking. But tokens were selected for positive shift, there is no zero-mean noise baseline, no RTN, no stochastic rounding, no weight-level bias correction, and </think> is not analysed; a penalty on hesitation tokens would also shorten an unquantized model, so this is not a causal separation of bias from size.

closest_papers.title: Quantization Inflates Reasoning: Token Inflation as a Hidden Cost of Low-Bit Reasoning Models
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Reports the RTN gap (Qwen3-4B INT4 average CTIR RTN +42.5% versus +4.7% to +12.0% for the others; Qwen3-30B RTN +43.0% versus +3.7% to +14.4%) but gives no explanation for it. No stochastic rounding, Gaussian weight noise or bias-correction control, and no measurement of weight MSE, output MSE, KL or perplexity, so CTIR is never regressed on any error size. 100 questions per benchmark, single temperature-0 run, no variance. Its only two citing papers (2610.34886 ThinkBit, 2610.05685) do not address the cause.

closest_papers.title: Quantized Reasoning Models Think They Need to Think Longer, but They Do Not
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Read main text and appendix. No random-noise control on weights, logits or activations, no stochastic rounding, no bias correction, no RTN. No signed logit shift at </think> or marker tokens is measured (KL only, which has no sign). The only 'random' control is "50 randomly selected tokens serving as a null control" for the penalty list. GPTQ 3-bit gives 6.8K tokens versus 23.4K for AWQ 3-bit against 5.2K at BF16 on MATH-500, again a same-width quantizer gap left unexplained. All 17 citing papers were listed; none adds the missing control.

closest_papers.title: How Divergence Becomes Decision Flips in Compressed Language Models
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Per-step, teacher-forced evidence for the 'size' reading: "every structured compressor's A lies within 0.915-1.005 of the null's" and "Standard compressors therefore perturb the decision margins like a generic direction of the same Fisher norm"; "At equal KL, isotropic noise yields a median 11% more total variation and 14% more flips than the measured compressors". RTN only, no stochastic rounding. It does not measure free generation or length; it says per-position statistics do not show "how changed decisions compound over free generation".

closest_papers.title: Halt Vector (arXiv 2608.28859)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: A magnitude-matched random-direction persistent offset lengthens thinking: 7,195 think-tokens versus 6,516 base (+10%) on train-24, +3% on AMC. Supports 'any persistent disturbance lengthens' but has no fresh per-step noise arm, no quantization or compression arm, and the random arm's drift was not measured ("it was scored against the halt axis rather than against its own").

closest_papers.title: Acceptance Is Not Speed (arXiv 2610.23818)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Unbiased token-level noise lengthens too (temperature 1.2: 1.27x on GSM8K, 1.07x on LiveCodeBench for GPT-OSS-20B; T=1.5: 3.9x), and the paper states it has no mechanism: "we do not explain why an unlikely token makes a reasoning model think longer." It does not separate a one-sided perturbation from unbiased noise of equal size and does not test quantization. First 100k characters read.

closest_papers.title: Spend Bytes on Breadth: Precision-Count Trade-offs for Decode-Time KV Compression in Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
closest_papers.what_it_shows: KV side. Eviction lengthens ("SnapKV-D outputs are 1.1-2.0x as long as FullKV's"), lower-bit KV quantization at equal bytes does not raise the capped share, and one codec writes 11% longer outputs although "the averaged single-step error we measure does not see it". Explanation is an untested hypothesis ("which we have not tested"). No round-to-nearest versus stochastic or dithered KV rounding, no bias-versus-size analysis.

closest_papers.title: Why Does Post-Training Quantization Work?
closest_papers.what_it_shows: NVFP4 RTN next-token analysis: errors partly cancel across layers and the LM head preserves high-ranked tokens. No matched-noise baseline, no bias/variance split, no stochastic rounding, no bias correction, no reasoning models; limitations say it does not address "how these mechanisms extend to multi-token generation". First 100k of 225k characters read.

closest_papers.title: Language model capabilities fail in a shared, predictable order under compression and perturbation
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Compares Gaussian weight noise, zeroing, ablation, layer removal with Wanda, SparseGPT and GPTQ at matched degradation, not matched size. Generation capped at "at most 32 new tokens"; no length or stopping measure; no RTN. Does not bear on the question beyond showing GPTQ does not follow the random-noise order across models (median 0.095).

closest_papers.title: Extreme Low-Bit Inference in Reasoning Models: Failure Modes and Targeted Recovery
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Documents loops, delayed commitment and unclosed thinking at W2 (GPTQ-style). Mechanism is a stated hypothesis only ("small perturbations introduced by low-bit inference can accumulate over long reasoning trajectories"). No </think> or EOS logit measurement, no noise, stochastic-rounding or bias-correction control.

closest_papers.title: RECAP: Calibrating Low-Bit Reasoning Models on the History They Read
closest_papers.what_it_shows: W4A4KV4-style setting; longer outputs are reported as an association ("Of the 101 questions that change from correct to incorrect, 96 produce longer quantized outputs") and the paper concedes "the table alone does not isolate this mechanism." No bias-versus-size split and no rounding or noise control.

closest_papers.title: Low-Discrepancy Dither for Quantized Recurrent State Caches (2609.39185) and Quantizing Recurrent Language Models Is Easier Than You Think (2611.01864)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Abstracts only. Both compare rounding rules (RTN, stochastic rounding, dither) on recurrent state, where RTN "discards small updates, its error keeps growing". Both are state-only; neither abstract reports reasoning length or a weight or KV rounding-rule comparison.

answered.remaining_gap:
No paper found measures, for weight quantization (or KV quantization, or eviction), whether reasoning-length inflation comes from a systematic signed component or from error size. The experiment that separates the two exists only for recurrent state (2611.12127), and that part of the card's question is answered: bias.

What is untouched for weights:
- No study runs RTN, an unbiased or bias-corrected variant, and matched-size Gaussian weight noise on the same model and reports generation length. 2610.00694 has the matched-noise arm but only teacher-forced flips. 2606.25519 and 2606.00206 have length but no control and no error-size measurement.
- Nobody has measured the signed logit shift at </think> under weight quantization. RATIO (2609.39801) measures signed shifts on hesitation tokens only, after selecting for positive sign.
- The RTN versus HQQ/GPTQ/AWQ gap at the same width (+42.5% versus +6.0% on Qwen3-4B) has not been regressed against output error, so it is unknown whether it is just an error-size gap.

Two things weaken the card even though it is not answered:
1. RATIO is missing from the card's evidence and already shows a same-sign shift on hesitation tokens shared by AWQ and GPTQ whose subtraction cuts CoT length 25.66-51.34%. A reviewer may read outcome A (score and correct the mean shift at marker logits) as partly published at the logit level; the new part would be only the weight-level cause and fix.
2. Published per-step and noise results lean toward 'size' or 'any disturbance lengthens': compressors move margins like a generic direction of equal Fisher norm (2610.00694), a random-direction offset lengthens +10% (2608.28859), and temperature 1.2 lengthens 1.27x (2610.23818). These make the 'always positive' sign explainable without bias, so the expert prediction is firmer than the card's 'medium'.

A design caveat that is my own reasoning, not from a paper: stochastic rounding of weights is done once, so each draw is still a fixed error with a fixed layer-output mean shift, and RTN weight error is already close to zero-mean per weight. The stochastic-rounding arm is therefore not the weight analogue of the state experiment and cannot remove a mean shift; only the bias-correction arm and the matched-Gaussian arm discriminate. The card's 'removable by unbiased/stochastic rounding' wording transfers to KV and state (re-rounded every step), not to weights.

evidence_checks.claim: 2611.12127: same-width bf16 stochastic rounding (SR) of recurrent state removes the length increase in four of five affected models; authors attribute it to bias, not resolution; weights not tested.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Read arXiv 2611.12127 HTML. Table 3 (FP32 / bf16 RTN / bf16 SR): Qwen3.5-9B caps 118 / 223 / 111, accuracy 85.6 / 70.8 / 87.6; SR/FP32 length x0.991 to x1.049. Abstract: "so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution." Only the state dtype changes between arms; weight and KV quantization not tested. But the mechanism the paper gives is specific to an accumulator: the state "is therefore re-rounded at every step, so any rounding bias can accumulate", and updates below about 2^-9 of the stored value are rounded away ("write erasure"). That is the textbook stagnation effect that SR is known to fix. A weight tensor is rounded once and never re-rounded, so this mechanism has no analogue there. The paper also notes FP16 RTN is much milder than bf16 RTN, so resolution matters too.

evidence_checks.claim: 2606.00206: weight-quantization explanation is noise at uncertain positions (Spearman 0.92 KL vs entropy); no random-noise or unbiased-rounding control; RTN not tested; explanation hedged as intuition.
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: Read arXiv 2606.00206 HTML (first 100k characters). Quantizers are GPTQ and AWQ at 3 and 4 bit, FlatQuant W4A4KV4 / W8A8KV8; no RTN. "Position-level KL divergence correlates strongly with the BF16 model's next-token entropy" (rho = 0.92, AWQ 3-bit only). "this argument provides intuition for one specific failure mode, not a complete causal explanation". No noise or SR control. Two things the card leaves out: (i) the paper reports a Spearman rho of -0.73 between accuracy change and CoT growth across 28 model-quantizer pairs, i.e. length tracks degradation size; (ii) the authors state the diagnostic is not specific to quantization and any weight or activation perturbation may act the same way, which is the size reading.

evidence_checks.claim: The average length change is positive in every published configuration (used in why_uncertain as evidence against a zero-mean disturbance).
evidence_checks.what_the_source_says: False across the literature. 2606.00206 Table 2 has average CoT decreases: Qwen-14B GPTQ W4 -308 tokens, Qwen-14B FlatQuant W8A8KV8 -330, Qwen-7B FlatQuant W8A8KV8 -73, Llama-8B GPTQ W4 -94. In 2606.25519 Table 2 the row averages are all positive but individual cells are negative for every non-RTN INT4 quantizer (Qwen3-4B AWQ GPQA-D -7.0, GSM8K -2.7; HQQ GPQA-D -2.2, LCB -1.2; Qwen3-30B GPTQ AIME25 -1.7, MBPP -0.8; HQQ BBH -0.8). premise.predicted_answer:
Size (outcome B), and I would bet about 4:1 on it for the weight case, which is the only case the first experiment tests.

Expected results per arm:
- **Stochastic rounding of weights:** inflates length as much as RTN or more, not less.
- **Matched Gaussian weight noise:** lands within the null-arm spread of RTN.
- **Bias-corrected RTN:** inflates somewhat less, by about as much as its output error and total variation fall. That is still the size reading, because the mean shift is one component of output squared error.
- **RTN versus HQQ gap:** disappears once arms are compared at matched teacher-forced total variation.

Where I am less sure (about 2:1): whether total variation alone predicts length for small perturbations on a large model. Qwen3-30B RTN inflates +43.0% with no accuracy loss (2606.25519), and 2611.12127 shows teacher-forced KL misranks state head groups.
premise.strongest_argument_it_is_boring:
The contradiction is between two different objects, and the one experiment that favours "bias" has a mechanism that cannot occur in weights.

1. **The state result is textbook stagnation.** 2611.12127 explains its own finding: the recurrent state is an accumulator that "is therefore re-rounded at every step", and updates below about 2^-9 of the stored value are rounded away. Stochastic rounding is the standard fix because it is re-drawn every step and averages out over time. A weight tensor is rounded once. One frozen stochastic-rounding draw is a fixed perturbation, exactly as persistent as RTN, and is "unbiased" only over draws nobody takes at inference.

2. **Stochastic rounding of weights is already known not to help.** It has about twice the squared error of RTN on a uniform grid (step²/6 versus step²/12). AdaRound (arXiv 2004.10568, Table 1) measured this: Nearest 52.29, Stochastic 52.06 ± 5.52 over 100 draws.

3. **RTN error already behaves like matched random noise.** With min-max groups of 128 and no clipping, RTN error is close to uniform and uncorrelated with the weight. 2610.00694 reports that RTN, GPTQ, AWQ and isotropic Gaussian weight noise "fall on the same curve" and "perturb the decision margins like a generic direction of the same Fisher norm". The RTN versus matched-Gaussian arm therefore has a strong prior of no difference.

4. **The card's two reasons for uncertainty do not hold.**
   - "Always positive" is false: 2606.00206 has four configurations with shorter CoT, and 2606.25519 has negative cells for every non-RTN INT4 quantizer.
   - Fresh unbiased noise lengthens anyway: temperature 1.2 gives 1.27x (2610.23818). Length has a floor and a heavy right tail of loops and cap hits, so a positive mean needs no bias.
   - The RTN-to-HQQ gap comes with an accuracy-drop gap of 11.3 versus 1.8 points on Qwen3-4B in the same paper, so it is an error-size gap.

5. **The dose-response is already in print.** 2504.04823 Sec. 4.1 has W4G128 matching BF16 length and W3G128 longer, more so in small models. 2606.00206 reports rho = -0.73 between accuracy change and CoT growth over 28 pairs. Lil has length falling as budget grows.

6. **The design question is ill-posed.** "Output squared error or mean shift" is not a choice: E||dW x||² with the uncentred Hessian that GPTQ uses already contains the mean-shift term. Bias compensation for LLM quantization is published (arXiv 2404.01892) and works by lowering output error.

Outcome B gives a number, not a method, as the card's own judge noted. The predicted outcome is therefore also the less useful one.
premise.sharpened_question:
Drop "bias versus size" for weights. What survives is the time structure of the error, plus the one unexplained number.

**Question.** At matched teacher-forced total variation, does closed-loop reasoning length depend on whether the perturbation is frozen for the whole trace or re-drawn during decoding?

- Frozen: one weight draw, KV entries quantized once at write, a deterministic eviction rule.
- Re-drawn: state stochastic rounding, resampled eviction, temperature.

Published data is split. Re-drawn error removes inflation for state (2611.12127) and raises accuracy for eviction (2606.03928, length not reported), but lengthens for temperature (2610.23818). No paper holds per-step size fixed and varies only persistence.

**Test on Qwen3-4B.**
- (a) One frozen Gaussian weight draw versus rotating among k independent draws every N tokens, at equal per-layer output error.
- (b) int4 KV with RTN versus stochastic rounding at write.
- (c) Deterministic versus resampled eviction at matched missing attention, reporting length.
- A null arm, and teacher-forced total variation for every arm.

**Readout.**
- If frozen and re-drawn inflate equally at matched total variation, total variation is the single offline predictor and residue (a) is answered.
- If re-drawn inflates less, the design is dithering or resampling for KV-side methods.

**Caveats.**
- I lean about 2:1 that persistence does not matter for weights.
- A positive result gives no cheap weight-side design, because re-drawing weights needs the full-precision weights or k copies.
- This is close to residue (a) with one added axis, not a new question.

**Side check.** Does Qwen3-30B RTN's +43.0% length with no accuracy loss (2606.25519) reproduce against a null arm? It is the only published number the size story does not obviously cover.

feasible.first_week_experiment:
The card's central arm is mis-specified, so the design below changes it. Stochastic rounding of weights is done once: a single draw is a fixed perturbation with about twice the weight squared error of round-to-nearest (step^2/6 against step^2/12), and nothing averages it out. It is not the analogue of stochastic rounding of a state that is re-rounded every step. The clean test for weights is to split the RTN error of each linear layer into its systematic part (the shift of the layer's output mean) and its zero-mean remainder, and run each alone.

MODEL: Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 (8 GB download; the model in 2606.25519 Table 2), INT4, group 128, weights stored dequantized in bf16 so stock vLLM 0.32 runs them at full speed. Greedy, thinking on, 32,768-token cap.

DATA: GSM8K 300, BBH 300, GPQA-Diamond 198 (all cached). Published targets for RTN on this model (2606.25519 Table 2, read this session): GSM8K 1139 -> 1548 (+35.9%), GPQA-D 7796 -> 10596 (+35.9%), BBH 2674 -> 5470 (+104.6%). MATH-500 is not in that table, so it is dropped from the first pass.

DAY 1, offline (under 0.1 GPU-day): (a) generate BF16 reference traces; (b) from 128 of them collect the input mean mu and second moment of every linear layer; (c) for RTN error dW per layer compute the share of output error energy that is mean shift, |dW mu|^2 / E|dW x|^2; (d) teacher-forced on 200 BF16 traces, measure total variation and the logit shift at the end-of-thinking token and at marker tokens (Wait, But, Alternatively) for RTN, mean-only and mean-removed weights.

ARMS (each a weight transform, about 100 lines of torch in total):
0. BF16 x3 with different request order and concurrency: the null spread.
1. RTN, asymmetric min-max; also symmetric min-max, because 2606.25519 does not state the range rule.
2. Dose-response: W + lambda*dW for lambda = 0.5, 0.71, 1.41.
3. Stochastic rounding on the same grid, 3 draws.
4. RTN error values permuted within each group of 128, 3 draws (identical error magnitudes, structure destroyed); Gaussian noise matched in per-layer output squared error, 2 draws.
5. Mean-removed RTN: dW - (dW mu) mu^T / |mu|^2 (off-grid, a diagnostic).
6. Mean-only: W + (dW mu) mu^T / |mu|^2 (full-precision weights plus only RTN's output-mean shift).
7. Optional: HQQ INT4 g128 as the low-inflation reference (published +6.0% average).

METRICS: per-question paired log length ratio against BF16 run 1 with bootstrap CI over questions; mean reasoning tokens (CTIR as defined in 2606.25519); cap hits; accuracy; marker rate per 1k tokens; and where each arm sits on the lambda dose-response curve at its measured output error.

COST: about 800 questions per arm is 2.5 to 4 million generated tokens; at the measured 526 to 2,024 tok/s that is 1.2 to 2 hours per arm on one A6000. About 20 runs.

DAYS 4-7 if the mean arms separate from the null: repeat arms 0, 1, 5, 6 on Qwen/Qwen3-8B (cached) and at T=0.6 with 4 samples; then int4 KV with round-to-nearest against stochastic rounding in the HF engine (kvfetch/sparse_decode.py, method full), where each token is rounded separately and the stochastic-rounding analogy to 2611.12127 actually holds.
feasible.result_that_kills_it:
Any one of these, all reachable by day 3:

1. Day 1, offline: the mean-shift part is a small share (a few percent or less) of each layer's RTN output error energy, and the teacher-forced logit shift at the end-of-thinking and marker tokens for the mean-only model is inside the BF16 null. Then there is no systematic component of meaningful size to blame.

2. Day 2: RTN does not reproduce an inflation clearly above the null spread (target: about +36% on GSM8K and GPQA-D, +105% on BBH). Then there is no effect to explain in this setup.

3. Day 2-3: the mean-only arm is within the null spread of BF16, the mean-removed arm is within the null spread of RTN, and permuted-error, matched-Gaussian and stochastic-rounding arms all fall on RTN's lambda dose-response curve at their own output error. Then size is the answer, there is no quantizer change to make, and what is left is an offline predictor (a number), which was already the known residue.

I expect outcome 3, at roughly 80%, higher than the card's judge (60-65%), for four reasons found while checking:
- The bias in 2611.12127 is "write erasure": an update smaller than about 2^-9 of the stored value is rounded away at every decode step, so the state stops moving. That mechanism needs an accumulator that is re-rounded thousands of times. Weights are rounded once. The card's "contradiction" is between two different kinds of object; the weight analogue (layer output-mean shift) is the card's own construction, not a claim in either paper.
- The same table that gives RTN +42.5% gives RTN an accuracy drop of 11.3 points on Qwen3-4B against 0.9 (GPTQ), 1.8 (HQQ), -0.7 (AWQ). RTN is simply a much larger error; the 7-10x inflation gap needs no bias story.
- "Never negative" holds only for averages. Per benchmark the table has AWQ INT4 at -7.0% on GPQA-D and -2.7% on GSM8K, HQQ at -2.2% and -1.2%, with one seed, 100 questions and no noise floor. HQQ's +6.0% and AWQ's +8.2% may be inside the noise.
- The card's own evidence says zero-mean disturbances lengthen reasoning (temperature 1.2 gives 1.27x; a random steering direction gives about 10%).
feasible.result_that_makes_it_a_paper:
The mean-only arm, which carries only RTN's per-layer output-mean shift and a small fraction of its output error energy, reproduces at least half of RTN's length inflation; and the mean-removed arm loses at least half of it while keeping nearly all of the squared error. Both gaps must be several times the BF16 null spread, hold on GSM8K, BBH and GPQA-D, repeat on Qwen3-8B and at T=0.6, and the teacher-forced logit shift at the end-of-thinking token must rank the arms in the same order as measured length. A second quantizer (the residual +12.0% of GPTQ or +8.2% of AWQ) shrinking under the same correction would make it general.

That would give: a causal account that no paper has for weights (2606.00206 says its margin argument is "not a complete causal explanation"; 2606.25519 only hypothesises that "small perturbations can accumulate across many decoding steps"), a one-vector-per-layer fix that costs nothing at run time, and a scoring rule for quantizers that is not squared error.

A weaker but still reportable middle result: the dose-response in lambda is sharply thresholded and stochastic rounding or permuted error sits clearly off the curve. That says error structure matters beyond size, without yet naming the structure.

feasible.follow_on_design_space:
Only if the systematic-part outcome holds (mean-only reproduces the inflation, mean-removed loses it):

1. Quantizer objective. Add a per-layer output-mean-shift term to GPTQ, AWQ or HQQ, computed on the model's own reasoning traces. On-grid version: choose round-up or round-down per weight to minimise squared error subject to dW mu = 0 (an AdaRound-style choice with one linear constraint per output channel). Deployable version: one bias vector per residual-stream writer (o_proj, down_proj), zero run-time cost; this also needs the small vLLM model-class change noted in the blockers.

2. Selection criterion. Score a quantizer offline by the mean hidden-state shift it causes, projected on the length-control direction (the halt direction of 2608.28859, or the logit of the end-of-thinking token), instead of perplexity or squared error. This is a direct attack on residue (a): one offline quantity that predicts length inflation. 2609.06473 reports that such directions survive quantization (cosine 0.945-0.990 for NF4) but never measured the shift along them.

3. Same split for the other lossy methods, where the analogy is tighter than for weights:
- KV quantization: each token is rounded separately, so a per-channel mean error exists across tokens; test round-to-nearest against stochastic rounding and against a per-channel mean correction at the same bits.
- KV eviction and sparse attention: dropping tokens removes a consistent share of attention output; compensate with a running mean-value token or a per-layer correction vector instead of raising the budget. This connects to the user's own H3 finding that minimum missing attention per step is not maximum accuracy, and to VaSE's unexplained gain from sampled retention.
- Sparse-attention drafts in speculative decoding (SparseSpec, PillarAttn): a mean-corrected draft should drift less from the target over the k draft steps, which is measurable as accepted length.
- FP8 and FP4 serving, and recurrent state in hybrids (2611.12127; the user's abl_ssm_bf16 runs under /home/ryankert_l/kv-fetch/kv-fetch/results/profile/harness/done).

4. Depth and placement. Which blocks' mean shift matters (last blocks only, per 2504.02010's final-layer sensitivity), which gives a mixed-precision rule driven by length rather than accuracy.

5. A general "length-neutral compression" correction: one learned or calibrated vector per layer that cancels the length shift of any lossy method, with the serving cost of longer chains (2606.25519: a 1.1x CTIR increase raises p90 TTFT from 1050 s to 1400 s) as the stated benefit.

If the size outcome holds instead, the design space is narrow: an offline predictor of inflation from teacher-forced total variation plus the lambda dose-response curve, and bit allocation per layer by length sensitivity. That answers residue (a) for the weight case only and is a measurement paper at best.

verified.question: What sets the time of a decode attention kernel when each request reads only a short KV list, and where is the knee below which reading more tokens costs nothing?

closest_papers.title: PersistentKV (decode attention with sequence splitting and a persistent work queue)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Closest paper to the card's fit. It publishes a per-request cost model for decode attention with all three of the card's terms: T_r = KVBytes/beta * max(1, Cmin/C_r) + L_r*lambda + MergeBytes_r/beta, fitted on an RTX 3060 against FlashInfer 0.2.5 with beta = 331.2 GB/s, Cmin = 4 CTAs per SM (the occupancy / stream-count term) and lambda = 8.19 us per kernel launch. It states the occupancy explanation directly: "Low-active decode does not expose enough CTAs if each request and KV head owns only one CTA. PersistentKV therefore splits the sequence dimension into S disjoint ranges". It also states the short-list result: "short-context steps below 16K tokens route to FlashInfer because split/merge overhead dominates", and "CUDA graph replay reduced Python launch mechanics but did not overcome the two-kernel decode-plus-merge cost on B4 ... the remaining B4 problem is not merely host overhead". Limits: contexts 8K-64K only, one consumer GPU, no lists of 64-2K tokens; "Non-RTX GPUs ... not measured". CARD CORRECTION: Table 4 gives FlashInfer 1.00 launches/step, PersistentKV buckets 16.00, PersistentKV work queue 2.00. The 16 -> 2 launch reduction is internal to PersistentKV, not relative to FlashInfer, so the small B8 gain does not show that launches are a minor term.

closest_papers.title: PAT: Accelerating LLM Decoding via Prefix-Aware Attention with Resource Efficient Multi-Tile Kernel (ASPLOS '26)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Publishes the latency-bound criterion that the card lists as an alternative explanation: "To saturate global memory bandwidth, the pipeline must keep enough data in flight to cover the inherent memory latency ... the flat region gives the inherent latency L (ns) and the linear region the sustainable bandwidth B (Bytes/ns). Thus the in-flight data D_flight must satisfy D_flight >= L x B", with D_flight = S*C*n*h*b. It also names a per-list fixed cost for short KV: "at KV length 192, n=128 yields (192-128)/128 ~ 50% compute bubble in the last tile, while n=64 removes it", and selects tile size by an offline sweep over KV length "encoded as a piecewise decision tree". Multi-stream forwarding "overlaps the launch overhead of subsequent kernels with the execution of preceding kernels". Limits: A100/H100 only, shared-prefix workloads; no fitted constant per call or per list and no knee for sparse lists at small batch.

closest_papers.title: Lean Attention: Hardware-Aware Scalable Attention Mechanism for the Decode-Phase of Transformers
closest_papers.what_it_shows: The card's expert prediction (too few independent streams, so split each list across thread blocks) is published here since 2024. It describes FlashAttention-2 decode as having "extremely low SM occupancy", says fixed-split schemes (FlashDecoding, FlashInfer) have "quantization inefficiencies", and uses Stream-K partitioning with an exact softmax merge in one launch, "avoiding the reduction kernel launch overheads that FlashDecoding suffers from". It does not study sparse or very short lists.

closest_papers.title: FlashInfer: Efficient and Customizable Attention Engine for LLM Inference Serving
closest_papers.what_it_shows: The baseline kernel already implements the card's proposed fix. The load-balanced scheduler is "inspired by Stream-K", "total number of CTAs is set to k x #SM", and "KV-splitting is only applied to requests that have large KV lengths. Requests with short KV lengths do not require splitting". The local source (/home/ryankert_l/subspec_v2/flashinfer_repo/include/flashinfer/attention/scheduler.cuh) confirms it: whenever batch*Hkv is below blocks_per_sm*num_sm the planner binary-searches a chunk size with a minimum of 128 tokens, and under CUDA graph it always uses the partition-kv kernel plus merge (two launches); without CUDA graph it skips splitting when no list exceeds the chunk. Table 5 shows short-prefix composable gain vanishing: prefix 1024, BS=16: 45.17 vs 46.52 us, with "Smaller values of n do not benefit from composable formats due to insufficient increase in block size". No decomposition of the ~45 us floor is given.

closest_papers.title: Inference Time Context Sparsity: Illusion or Opportunity?
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Source of the anomaly; numbers on the card verified in Table 1 (H100, 128K context, Hq=32, Hkv=8, page 16). At B=1 FlashInfer dense is 0.19 ms and the sparse speedup saturates: 100x sparsity 10.25, 200x 11.05, 500x 11.14. At B=16 (3.08 ms dense) 100x 20.09, 200x 37.32, 500x 76.77. By my arithmetic the B=1 floor is about 17 us and B=16 at 500x is about 40 us, i.e. roughly a 15-17 us constant plus about 1.5 us per request. The paper reports the plateau and does not explain or decompose it.

closest_papers.title: SparseSpec: Accelerating Large Language Model Reasoning with Self-Speculative Sparse Attention (PillarAttn)
closest_papers.what_it_shows: The card's second anomaly already has a stated explanation in the source. "the kernel optimized for verification (full) attention achieves near 85% bandwidth but less than 50% for draft (sparse) attention; kernels optimized for sparse attention deliver over 80% bandwidth, but degrade to 50% on full attention", attributed to "different arithmetic intensities due to different input token counts, leading to different best kernel implementations (e.g., tile sizes and MMA instruction)". The fused kernel gain is attributed to "(2) higher bandwidth utilization when having more transaction bytes within a single kernel to overlap pipeline latency" -- the latency-bound explanation, named but not quantified. "reduces the execution time of Attention by 3.29x" verified.

closest_papers.title: Where Activation Sparsity and KV-Cache Sparsity Cross in LLM Decoding
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Only paper found that times a shortened KV read on the researcher's class of card. With flash-attn 2.6.3 split-K at batch 1, a 30%-keep gathered contiguous KV selection "runs within 1% of its byte bound on RTX A6000 and within 6% on A100"; extra kernel cost beyond byte time is "at most 0.3 ms" per whole decode step on RTX A6000 (Llama-3.1-8B, 32 layers; about 10 us per layer or less by my arithmetic) and within 0.8 ms on A100. Dense steps move "0.72 TB/s" on RTX A6000. Limits: batch 1 only, lists of 600 tokens and up, contiguous gathered lists rather than paged irregular ones, fixed cost reported as one lump.

closest_papers.title: Memory-Bound but Not Bandwidth-Limited: The Physical AI Inference Gap in Batch-1 LLM Decode
closest_papers.what_it_shows: Measures a short-list per-call floor directly on H100 at batch 1, kv_len 2049, Llama-3-8B GQA shape: "PyTorch's default SDPA dispatcher (36.05 us/layer) outperforms explicit FLASH_ATTENTION context (44.35 us), FlashInfer (48.20 us) and FlashAttention-3 (79.25 us) at H100 batch-1 single-decode shape; the kernel choice is not the binding constraint." By my arithmetic the KV bytes at that shape are about 8.4 MB, about 2.5 us at H100 peak bandwidth, so roughly 45 us of the 48 us is not byte time. The paper attributes the short-context H100 gap to "the launch of the many small kernels" and shows CUDA graphs give 1.259x on H100 but 1.028x on L4. It says "We do not claim the launch-bound observation itself is novel; CUDA Graphs and launch-bound regimes are folk knowledge among kernel engineers." Limits: batch 1 only, single-decode API (host call time included), no sparse lists, no batch sweep, no decomposition into per-call vs per-list. Read in part (abstract, intro, related work, start of section 6).
